question: An Agentforce is creating a custom action in Agent. Which option is available for the Agentforce Specialist to choose for the custom copilot action?
optionA: Apex trigger
optionB: SOQL
optionC: Flows
explanation:
Flows are the option available for a custom action in Agent. When creating a custom action, one of the available options is to use Flows: a declarative automation tool that lets the Agentforce Specialist define custom logic and actions within the Copilot system, extending its functionality without custom code. Flows are the recommended method for creating custom actions within Agent because they are declarative and highly adaptable.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Apex trigger) — a trigger fires on a DML event, not on an agent's request; it is not an action type an agent can invoke, and Apex only enters an agent as an invocable method, not as a trigger.
Option B (SOQL) — a query language, not an action type; there is no way to register a raw SOQL statement as a custom copilot action.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.copilot_actions_custom.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Before activating a custom Agent action, an Agentforce Specialist would like to understand multiple real- world user utterances to ensure the action is being selected appropriately. Which tool should the Specialist recommend?
optionA: Agentforce
optionB: Agent Builder
optionC: Model Playground
explanation:
Agent Builder is the one option here that lets the Specialist evaluate real-world utterances: its Preview panel lets you test the agent by inputting utterances, and the canvas shows which subagents were selected and the reasoning behind the selection.
The tool Salesforce documents for evaluating many real-world utterances at once is Agentforce Testing Center, which batch-tests subagent and action selection from a CSV of scenarios. It is not among the options here. Treat this item as defective rather than subtle: the best answer to the question as written is Testing Center, and this option set omits it; a near-duplicate of this question elsewhere in the deck does offer Testing Center and keys it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Agentforce) — the product family as a whole, not a tool; it names nothing you can open to observe which action an utterance selects.
Option C (Model Playground) — not an agent-testing tool. It belongs to AI Models (formerly Einstein Studio) and the Bring Your Own LLM flow: you evaluate a foundation model's response to your prompts under different settings before deploying that model to production. It says nothing about whether an agent selects the right action for a given utterance.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.agent_builder_tour.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.agent_testing_center.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=data.c360_a_ai_foundation_models.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: C->B. Model Playground evaluates a foundation model's responses in the Bring Your Own LLM flow, not an agent's action selection, so the original key named the wrong tool. The item is also defective: the documented answer for evaluating multiple real-world utterances is Agentforce Testing Center, which this option set omits (its near-duplicate 63afa960 offers it and keys it). B is the best available option — Agent Builder's Preview panel tests utterances and shows which subagents and actions were selected, and why.

question: Universal Containers (UC) would like to implement the Sales Development Representative (SDR) Agent. Which channel consideration should UC be aware of while implementing it?
optionA: SDR Agent must be deployed in the Messaging channel.
optionB: SDR Agent only works in the Email channel.
optionC: SDR Agent must also be deployed on the company website.
explanation:
That the SDR Agent only works in the Email channel is the consideration to be aware of. The SDR agent, renamed Agentforce Lead Nurturing, runs on email, not Messaging. Its setup connects the agent user record to an email account so the agent can send and receive email, and its documented constraints are email constraints: up to 1,800 emails a day on a Gmail account and 9,800 on Microsoft Exchange, after which the agent stops sending for the day.
Note the naming: Salesforce renamed Agentforce SDR to Agentforce Lead Nurturing to distinguish it from the Lead Generation agent, so current articles are filed under the new name while the exam still says SDR.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (must be deployed in the Messaging channel) — no Messaging deployment step exists for this agent; it engages leads over email.
Option C (must also be deployed on the company website) — nothing in its setup requires a website deployment; the agent works from the connected mailbox.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.sales_agent_sdr_intro.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.sales_agent_sdr_setup_connect_agent_user_email.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: A->B. The SDR agent (now Agentforce Lead Nurturing) is set up by connecting an email account to the agent user so it can send and receive email, and its documented limits are email sending limits. No Messaging-channel deployment exists for it, so the original key described a channel the agent does not use.

question:
Universal Containers is very concerned about security compliance and wants to understand:
Which prompt text is sent to the large language model (LLM).
How it is masked.
The masked response.
What should the Agentforce Specialist recommend?
optionA: Ingest the Einstein Shield Event logs into CRM Analytics.
optionB: Review the debug logs of the running user.
optionC: Enable audit trail in the Einstein Trust Layer.
explanation:
Enabling the audit trail in the Einstein Trust Layer is what gives Universal Containers visibility into the prompt text sent to the LLM, how it is masked, and the masked response. The audit trail captures and logs the prompts sent to the large language model along with the masking of sensitive information and the AI's response, which is exactly the transparency a security compliance review needs.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (ingest Einstein Shield Event logs into CRM Analytics) — Shield event monitoring records system events such as logins and API calls, not the prompt text, masking or response of an individual generation.
Option B (review the debug logs of the running user) — Apex debug logs show code execution; they contain no view of AI prompt masking or of the LLM's response.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.generative_ai_audit_trail.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Choose 1 option. Universal Containers has multiple Salesforce orgs, each with a unique customer service agent where a verification agent must pass customer identity data to downstream agents handling account modifications. The customer ID must remain secure and persistent across agent handoffs without exposure to large language model (LLM) modification. What is the most appropriate configuration?
optionA: Implement a custom object to temporarily store verification status and have each agent query it via SOQL actions during execution.
optionB: Store customer identity information in conversation variables created by the first agent and have other agents read those same conversation variables.
optionC: Use the Agent API to start the downstream agent's session and pass the verified customer ID as a read- only context variable, ensuring security and preventing LLM alteration.
explanation:
Using the Agent API to start the downstream agent's session and pass the verified customer ID as a read-only context variable is the documented way to hand verified identity to another agent, and the reason is the variable model. When you start a session you can pass context variables and custom variables, and Salesforce documents that many variables are read-only and can only be set during the start session call: context variables carrying the $Context prefix are not editable after the session has started, with the single exception of $Context.EndUserLanguage. A customer ID passed that way is therefore fixed for the life of the session and cannot be rewritten by the model mid-conversation.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (custom object queried via SOQL actions) — puts the identity back into the agent's reasoning loop, where it is only as reliable as the action the planner happens to select; nothing makes it persistent or tamper-proof across the handoff.
Option B (conversation variables created by the first agent) — ordinary conversation variables are editable during the conversation and do not cross into another agent's session, so they neither persist across the handoff nor resist modification.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/ai/agentforce/guide/agent-api-variables.html

question: Choose 1 option. Universal Containers deploys a new Agentforce Service Agent into the company's website but is getting feedback that the Service Agent is not providing answers to customer questions that are found in the company's Salesforce Knowledge articles. What is the likely issue?
optionA: The Agentforce Service Agent user was not given the Allow View Knowledge permission set.
optionB: The Agentforce Service Agent user is not assigned the correct Agent Type License.
optionC: The Agentforce Service Agent user needs to be created under the standard Agent Knowledge profile.
explanation:
The Agentforce Service Agent user not having the Allow View Knowledge permission set is the likely issue. Reading knowledge articles is a Salesforce permission, and the agent user needs it like any other user: Lightning Knowledge user access documents that reading and searching published knowledge articles requires the Allow View Knowledge permission, so an agent user without it grounds on nothing and answers as though the articles do not exist. That is exactly the symptom described.
The fix follows from how Salesforce creates these users: the agent user starts with minimal access so the agent is secure by default, and you expand its access deliberately, based on the principle of least privilege. Granting knowledge read access is one of those deliberate expansions.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (not assigned the correct Agent Type License) — the agent type license governs which agent template and features are available, not article-level read access.
Option C (created under the standard Agent Knowledge profile) — there is no standard Agent Knowledge profile that an agent user must be created under.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.knowledge_setup_users_lex.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.agent_user.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A data scientist needs to view and manage models in Einstein Studio, and also needs to create prompt templates in Prompt Builder. Which permission sets should an Agentforce Specialist assign to the data scientist?
optionA: Prompt Template Manager and Prompt Template User
optionB: Data Cloud Admin and Prompt Template Manager
optionC: Prompt Template User and Data Cloud Admin
explanation:
Data Cloud Admin and Prompt Template Manager are the two permission sets, because two different jobs need two different grants. Managing models is a Data Cloud permission: model management in AI Models (the tool the exam calls Einstein Studio) is granted through the Data Cloud permission sets, which is why an admin-level Data Cloud permission set belongs in the answer. Creating prompt templates is a Prompt Builder permission, and Salesforce lists Prompt Template Manager as the permission required to create or modify prompt templates.
Two naming notes for anyone checking this against current documentation: Einstein Studio is now AI Models, its model-building tool is AI Model Builder, and the permission set granting admin-level access to all AI Models features is currently named Data Cloud Architect. The exam-era names are the ones in the options here.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Prompt Template Manager and Prompt Template User) — neither Prompt Builder permission grants access to models, so the data scientist could not view or manage anything in Einstein Studio.
Option C (Prompt Template User and Data Cloud Admin) — Prompt Template User only lets someone use an existing template, so this pairing leaves the data scientist unable to author one.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=data.c360_a_ai_license_perms.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.copilot_actions_custom.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Choose 1 option. Universal Containers (UC) is preparing to use the Agentforce Testing Center to ensure the reliability of a new agent. UC has a CSV file with test cases and is reviewing the documentation to understand best practices and limitations. Which best practice should the company follow to avoid modifying CRM data while running tests in the Testing Center?
optionA: Run tests in the production environment to ensure real-time data accuracy.
optionB: Limit the number of test cases to 50 per test to minimize data changes.
optionC: Use the Testing Center only in the sandbox environment.
explanation:
Using the Testing Center only in the sandbox environment is the practice Salesforce states directly on the Testing Center page: testing agents can modify CRM data, so use Testing Center only in your sandbox environment. That is the whole answer; the risk being avoided is a test run writing to live records.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (run tests in production for real-time data accuracy) — this is the thing the documentation warns against, not a way to ensure accuracy; production is where the modified CRM data would be live.
Option B (limit to 50 test cases per test) — capping a run does not make writes safer; Testing Center is built for large-scale batch runs, and the number of cases has no bearing on whether the org they touch is production.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.agent_testing_center.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Choose 1 option. Universal Containers (UC) recently attended a major trade show and received thousands of new leads from event badge scans. UC is struggling to follow up with each lead in a timely, personalized way. Leadership wants to: Qualify and nurture leads 24/7. * Provide accurate answers to prospect questions. * Automatically book meetings with qualified prospects. * Free up reps to focus on building relationships and closing deals. Which Agentforce capability should UC implement to meet these goals?
optionA: SDR Agent
optionB: Sales Coach
optionC: Commerce Agent
explanation:
The SDR Agent is the Agentforce capability that qualifies and nurtures thousands of new leads 24/7, provides accurate and consistent responses to prospects, schedules meetings for qualified leads, and frees sales reps to focus on relationship building and closing deals. Salesforce describes Agentforce SDR as helping sales teams qualify and nurture leads at scale, around the clock: it acts as a digital sales development representative that engages new leads instantly, asks qualifying questions, answers inquiries using connected Salesforce data, and automatically schedules meetings on behalf of the sales team, freeing human reps for high-value interactions rather than manual lead qualification. Note that Salesforce has since renamed Agentforce SDR to Agentforce Lead Nurturing; the exam still uses the SDR name.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Sales Coach) — coaches sales representatives internally with practice pitches and feedback; it does not engage prospects or book meetings.
Option C (Commerce Agent) — built for e-commerce use cases such as assisting shoppers with product discovery and order management, not lead nurturing.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.sales_agent_sdr_intro.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers is building a digital shopping assistant that needs to dynamically generate product recommendations using information from the company's external product recommendation predictive model through APIs. Which Agentforce capability should make it easier for the agent to consume the external product recommendation tool?
optionA: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
optionB: Hugging Face
optionC: Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol
explanation:
Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the Agentforce capability that makes an external tool easy for the agent to consume. MCP is an open standard that lets AI applications interact with external systems and services through pre-built connections instead of a bespoke integration per tool. In Agentforce you register a third-party MCP server in the Agentforce Registry and allowlist the server tools you want your agents to use, which is what makes an external recommendation model easy for the agent to call.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Hugging Face) — a model host, not a mechanism for an agent to discover and call a tool.
Option C (Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol) — governs communication between agents, not an agent's consumption of an external predictive model exposed over an API.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.agent_mcp_connect_register.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/ai/agentforce/guide/mcp.html

question: What is the primary function of the planner service in the Agent system?
optionA: Generating record queries based on conversation history
optionB: Offering real-time language translation during conversations
optionC: Identifying copilot actions to respond to user utterances
explanation:
Identifying copilot actions to respond to user utterances is the planner service's primary function: planning is action selection. Salesforce describes the path of a user message as an iterative classification and reasoning process: the agent first classifies the message into the best-matching subagent, then analyses the available information to decide its next step, which may be running an agent action that calls an Apex class, flow, or prompt template, asking a clarifying question, or answering directly.
One naming note: what the exam calls the planner service is documented today as the Atlas reasoning engine, and in metadata it is the planner bundle that contains an agent's topics and actions.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (generating record queries from conversation history) — that is something a selected action does, not the planning step itself.
Option B (real-time language translation) — a separate language capability rather than the function of the planner.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.agent_reasoning_engine.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) wants to improve the efficiency of addressing customer questions and reduce agent handling time with AI- generated responses. The agents should be able to leverage their existing knowledge base and identify whether the responses are coming from the large language model (LLM) or from Salesforce Knowledge. Which step should UC take to meet this requirement?
optionA: Turn on Service AI Grounding, Grounding with Case, and Service Replies.
optionB: Turn on Service Replies, Service AI Grounding, and Grounding with Knowledge.
optionC: Turn on Service AI Grounding and Grounding with Knowledge.
explanation:
Turning on Service Replies, Service AI Grounding, and Grounding with Knowledge is the step, because grounding alone drafts nothing. Service Replies is the feature that uses generative AI to draft replies for reps during chat and messaging sessions, and Salesforce's own instruction is to add grounding to Service Replies with Service AI Grounding, so reducing handling time with AI-generated responses needs Service Replies turned on as well as grounding.
The grounding half then decides where the content comes from. You turn on Service AI Grounding and select the sources: grounding with Knowledge has Einstein use your knowledge articles to draft responses, and it is what lets a rep see the article behind a drafted reply rather than guessing whether the wording came from the model or from the knowledge base.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Service AI Grounding, Grounding with Case, and Service Replies) — Grounding with Case grounds on case details, which is not the knowledge base this question asks about.
Option C (Service AI Grounding and Grounding with Knowledge) — without Service Replies this leaves the org with a grounding configuration and no generated replies to ground.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=service.einstein_replies_intro.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=service.einstein_generative_ai_enable_grounding.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=service.einstein_generative_ai_ground_knowledge.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: C->B. Service AI Grounding and Grounding with Knowledge configure what a reply is grounded on, but they do not generate replies. Salesforce documents Service Replies as the feature that drafts responses for reps and says to add grounding to Service Replies with Service AI Grounding, so all three are required for AI-generated replies drawn from the knowledge base. The deck's own explanation already argued for B while the key said C.

question: Universal Containers (UC) wants to make a marketing newsletter and directly use data from five unrelated objects (two standard and three custom) in a prompt template. How should UC accomplish this?
optionA: Create a Flex template and use the five objects as inputs.
optionB: Create a prompt template passing in a special custom object that connects the records temporarily.
optionC: Create a prompt#template#triggered flow to access the data from five objects.
explanation:
Creating a Flex template and using the five objects as inputs is how UC does it. A flex prompt template is the type Salesforce documents for any use case the other template types do not cover, and it is the one where you define the inputs yourself. In a flex template you add resources, the objects the prompt draws on, and the builder allows up to 5 of them, which is exactly what five unrelated objects, standard or custom, requires. Each resource gets its own name and API name and can be marked required.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (a special custom object that connects the records temporarily) — no bridging object is needed, since the template accepts the five objects directly as separate resources.
Option C (a prompt-template-triggered flow) — not a prompt template type at all; building one would not change what data the template can accept.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.prompt_builder_create_flex_prompt_template.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.prompt_builder_standard_template_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has implemented Generative AI within Salesforce to enable summarization of a custom object called Guest. Users have reported mismatches in the generated information. In refining its prompt design strategy, which key practices should UC prioritize?
optionA: Enable prompt test mode, allocate different prompt variations to a subset of users for evaluation, and standardize the most effective model based on performance feedback.
optionB: Create concise, clear, and consistent prompt templates with effective grounding, contextual role- playing, clear instructions, and iterative feedback.
optionC: Submit a prompt review case to Salesforce and conduct thorough testing In the playground to refine outputs until they meet user expectations.
explanation:
Creating concise, clear, and consistent prompt templates with effective grounding, contextual role-playing, clear instructions, and iterative feedback is the practice to prioritise, because it follows Salesforce's documented best practices for prompt design. Each element addresses the mismatch problem directly:
Effective grounding: ensuring the prompt pulls data from the correct sources.
Contextual role-playing: giving the AI a clear understanding of its role in generating the summary.
Clear instructions: unambiguous directions on what to include in the response.
Iterative feedback: regularly testing and adjusting prompts based on user feedback.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (prompt test mode with variations allocated to user subsets) — an evaluation technique, and no such user-allocation feature exists in Prompt Builder; it does not refine the prompt design itself.
Option C (submit a prompt review case to Salesforce and test in the playground) — Salesforce support does not review customer prompt designs; a support case suits technical faults, not general design refinement.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.prompt_builder_best_practices.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) needs to capture and store detailed interaction data for all agents. Which feature should help UC get a full view of the agent's behavior from start to finish, including reasoning engine executions, actions, prompt and gateway inputs/outputs, error messages, and final responses?
optionA: Agentforce Analytics
optionB: Utterance Analysis
optionC: Agentforce Session Tracing
explanation:
Agentforce Session Tracing is the feature built for exactly this list. It ingests data from the reasoning engine and other sources and combines it under a session ID, and Salesforce describes the log as covering turn-by-turn interactions, reasoning engine executions, actions, prompt and gateway inputs and outputs, error messages, and final responses. The trace data lands in a data model you can query and report on to investigate incidents and behaviour patterns.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Agentforce Analytics) — no Agentforce Analytics feature provides the end-to-end execution log described here; analytics reports on aggregate outcomes, not per-session traces.
Option B (Utterance Analysis) — looks at what users said and how those utterances were matched, not at the internal execution of a session.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.generative_ai_session_trace_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An administrator is responsible for ensuring the security and reliability of Universal Containers' (UC) CRM data. UC needs enhanced data protection and up-to-date AI capabilities. UC also needs to include relevant information from a Salesforce record to be merged with the prompt. Which feature in the Einstein Trust Layer best supports UC's need?
optionA: Data masking
optionB: Dynamic grounding with secure data retrieval
optionC: Zero-data retention policy
explanation:
Dynamic grounding with secure data retrieval is the Einstein Trust Layer feature that supports UC's need, because it is the one that merges relevant Salesforce record data into the prompt. Dynamic grounding means the AI dynamically retrieves relevant information from Salesforce records (customer records, case data, or custom object data) in a secure manner, so the generated output is contextually aware, aligned with real-time CRM data, and protected during AI processing.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Data masking) — obscures sensitive data for privacy purposes before it reaches the model; it does not merge Salesforce records into prompts.
Option C (Zero-data retention policy) — ensures the LLM provider does not store any user data after processing, but does not address the need to merge Salesforce record information into a prompt.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.generative_ai_trust_arch.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question:
When a verified customer in a help center says, "I want to upgrade my service plan," an AI agent needs to complete the following tasks:
Verify identity and entitlement.
Create a new quote.
Calculate a prorated upgrade amount.
Escalate to an Account Executive (AE) only if the reorder exceeds USD 25,000.
Which type of agent should an Agentforce Specialist build to support this use case?
optionA: Service Agent to resolve the case end-to-end and create a new opportunity for the sales team
optionB: Sales Agent to handle the upsell and large-deal escalation
optionC: Employee Agent to orchestrate internal logistics and finance
explanation:
A Service Agent that resolves the case end-to-end and creates a new opportunity for the sales team is the agent type to build. Start from the agent types Salesforce actually documents: Employee Agent, Lead Nurturing (formerly SDR), Sales Coach, Service Agent, Service Assistant, and the Setup agent. The scenario is a customer-facing self-service conversation that has to escalate when it exceeds a threshold, and that is the Service Agent: Salesforce describes it as intelligently supporting customers with common inquiries and escalating complex issues, deployable to an Experience Cloud site with built-in authentication. Identity and entitlement checks, quote creation and the prorated calculation are custom actions on that agent, and the escalation above USD 25,000 is a branch in its instructions.
One caveat about the wording: the option talks about creating an opportunity for the sales team, while the requirement is a quote. The discriminator is the agent type, not the record the escalation creates.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Sales Agent for the upsell and escalation) — there is no general-purpose Sales Agent type to build; the sales-side agents are Prospecting, Engagement and Sales Coach, which work leads and coach reps rather than serve an existing, verified customer in a help center.
Option C (Employee Agent for internal logistics and finance) — an Employee Agent serves internal users; this conversation is with a customer in a help center.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.agent_setup_explore_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=experience.support_add_agent_to_site.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: B->A. Salesforce's agent type table has no Sales Agent to build — the sales agents are Lead Nurturing, Prospecting, Engagement and Sales Coach, all of which work prospects or coach reps rather than serve a verified customer in a help center. The Service Agent is the documented customer-facing type, supports Experience Cloud with built-in authentication, and escalates complex issues, so it is the type this scenario calls for. Note that both option tails are loose: the requirement is a quote, and option A says opportunity.

question: What is true of Agentforce Testing Center?
optionA: Running tests risks modifying CRM data in a production environment.
optionB: Running tests does not consume Einstein Requests.
optionC: Agentforce Testing Center can only be used in a production environment.
explanation:
That running tests risks modifying CRM data in a production environment is the keyed answer, and it is true: a test really executes the agent's actions, so tests pointed at production can change live records — which is why sandbox is the place to run them.
Be aware that this item now has two true options. Until Summer '26, test runs consumed Einstein Requests, which made option B false. Salesforce's Considerations for Testing Center now says: "As of Summer '26, testing in Agentforce Testing Center is unmetered and doesn't consume Einstein Requests or Flex Credits", covering all test types, test creation, agent actions run by tests and result evaluation; only Data 360 queries made by tests are still metered. On a current org, B is also correct.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (does not consume Einstein Requests) — true as of Summer '26, as explained above; the exam predates the change and keys A.
Option C (can only be used in production) — inverts the guidance; Testing Center is not restricted to production, and sandbox is where tests belong.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.agent_testing_center.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.agent_testing_center_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Summer '26 made option B true as well. Considerations for Testing Center now says testing "is unmetered and doesn't consume Einstein Requests or Flex Credits" (only Data 360 queries from tests are still metered), so the previous explanation's reason for rejecting B no longer holds. A is still true and stays the key. History: the 2026-08-17 pass moved this key B->A when test runs did consume Einstein Requests.

question: Cloud Kicks (CK) is launching a new partner portal on Experience Cloud. CK wants to provide partners with an agent that can answer questions about product specifications from the knowledge base and allow them to submit a new Lead for a potential customer they've identified. The agent must be accessible only to authenticated partner users on the portal. Which agent type is required to meet this scenario?
optionA: Sales Agent
optionB: Commerce Agent
optionC: Service Agent
explanation:
The Service Agent is the agent type both requirements land on. Salesforce describes that type as intelligently supporting customers with common inquiries and escalating complex issues, and documents adding an Agentforce Service Agent to an Experience Cloud site as a self-service portal with built-in authentication, which is what restricts the agent to authenticated partner users on the portal.
Answering product questions from the knowledge base is the Answer Questions with Knowledge action grounded on published articles, and submitting a lead is a custom action built on a flow or Apex, so one agent covers both without changing type.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Sales Agent) — the sales-side agents work prospects and coach reps rather than serving partners in a portal, and there is no general-purpose Sales Agent type to deploy to an Experience Cloud site.
Option B (Commerce Agent) — belongs to the buying experience on an e-commerce channel, not a partner knowledge-and-lead portal.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=experience.support_add_agent_to_site.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.agent_setup_explore_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.copilot_actions_custom.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Choose 1 option. A developer is using the Salesforce CLI to deploy agent components from a sandbox to production. They recently made a change to several topics, instructions, and actions. Which metadata component should the developer include in their package.xml file that contains all of the topics and actions an agent will interact with?
optionA: genAiPlannerBundle
optionB: EinsteinAiPlannerBundle
optionC: BotBundle
explanation:
genAiPlannerBundle is the component to include. The Metadata API defines GenAiPlannerBundle as a planner for an agent or agent template and, in its own words, a container for all the topics and actions used to interact with a large language model, which is precisely what a deployment touching changed topics, instructions and actions needs to carry across. It has the .genAiPlannerBundle suffix, lives in a per-agent subfolder of genAiPlannerBundles, and is available in API version 64.0 and later.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (EinsteinAiPlannerBundle) — not a real metadata type; no such component exists in the Metadata API.
Option C (BotBundle) — not the agent planner and not a metadata type either; an agent's conversational shell is represented by Bot and BotVersion, which reference the planner rather than containing the topics and actions themselves.

https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_genaiplannerbundle.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) is implementing generative AI and wants to leverage a prompt template to provide responses to customers that gives personalized product recommendations to website visitors based on their browsing history. Which initial step should UC take to ensure the chatbot can deliver accurate recommendations?
optionA: Design universal product recommendations.
optionB: Write a response scrip for the chatbot.
optionC: Collect and analyze browsing data.
explanation:
Collecting and analyzing browsing data is the initial step, because personalized recommendations depend on understanding user behaviour, which requires structured data about browsing history. Without that data the model lacks the context needed to generate relevant suggestions. UC must first aggregate browsing data (pages visited, products viewed, session duration) into a dataset that reflects user preferences, then analyse it to find the patterns (frequently viewed categories, for example) that inform how the prompt should be structured. Salesforce prompt templates rely on grounding data to generate accurate outputs, and without analysed browsing data the template has nothing meaningful to ground personalization on.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (design universal product recommendations) — universal recommendations ignore personalization, which is the core requirement.
Option B (write a response script for the chatbot) — addresses chatbot interaction design, not the accuracy of the recommendations themselves.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.generative_ai_trust_arch.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Choose 1 option. Universal Containers (UC) is setting up a new Agentforce Service Agent. The company has sensitive medical product research stored internally and wants to ensure the agent cannot access it. What should UC da?
optionA: Assign the Agentforce Service Agent user the lowest possible role in the organization's hierarchy to block access.
optionB: Disable the Agentforce Service Agent's ability to use any Salesforce custom object or related fields.
optionC: Follow the principle of least privilege and avoid granting permission to view the Medical Product object or related
explanation:
Following the principle of least privilege and never granting permission to view the Medical Product object or its fields is what Salesforce's guidance for agent access prescribes: the agent user is created with minimal access so that the agent is secure by default, and you expand that access to support your use cases based on the principle of least privilege. Keeping sensitive medical research out of reach therefore means simply never granting the agent user permission to view that object or its fields.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (assign the agent user the lowest role in the hierarchy) — role hierarchy position governs record-level sharing, not object permissions, so a low role does not stop an agent user whose profile or permission set grants access to the object.
Option B (disable the agent's ability to use any custom object) — blanket-disabling every custom object would break the legitimate parts of the agent along with the sensitive one, and is not how object access is configured.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.agent_user.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers wants to keep retrieval accurate as product documentation changes frequently. Which approach should the company implement?
optionA: Leave embedding unchanged even if content is updated.
optionB: Rebuild the search index.
optionC: Manually delete the stale data chunks.
explanation:
Rebuilding the search index is the approach, because retrieval is only as good as the index behind it, so when the source content changes the index has to reflect that. Salesforce lets you trigger a full rebuild of a search index configuration from the search index list page or the object record view, and the rebuild reprocesses the content of the data model object, which is what restores accurate retrieval after documentation churn.
Worth knowing alongside the answer: indexing is not purely manual. After the initial build, a search index picks up new and modified records incrementally, so a full rebuild is the heavier remedy rather than a routine chore.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (leave embeddings unchanged after content is updated) — guarantees the retriever keeps serving the old text.
Option C (manually delete the stale data chunks) — not an exposed operation, and it would leave the index inconsistent with its source.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=data.c360_a_search_index_rebuild_search_index.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers' data science team is hosting a generative large language model (LLM) on Amazon Web Services (AWS). What should the team use to access externally-hosted models in the Salesforce Platform?
optionA: Model Builder
optionB: App Builder
optionC: Copilot Builder
explanation:
Model Builder is the tool for models that live outside Salesforce. Bring Your Own Model connects models built on external platforms, Amazon SageMaker among them, to Salesforce with a zero-copy approach, so no data is duplicated, and Bring Your Own Large Language Model does the same for a foundation model hosted externally, adding it as a model configuration you can then use for generative AI.
A naming note for current documentation: this tool is now AI Model Builder, formerly Einstein Studio Model Builder, and it sits under Data 360.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (App Builder) — assembles Lightning pages; it has no facility for connecting an externally hosted model.
Option C (Copilot Builder) — configures an agent's topics and actions; it does not register a model.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=data.c360_a_ai_license_perms.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=data.c360_a_bring_your_own_model.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) needs to improve the agent productivity in replying to customer chats. Which generative AI feature should help UC address this issue?
optionA: Case Summaries
optionB: Service Replies
optionC: Case Escalation
explanation:
Service Replies is the generative AI feature that improves agent productivity in replying to customer chats. It drafts accurate, contextual replies for customer service agents during chat and messaging sessions, using past interactions, case data, and the context of the conversation, so reps review and send rather than compose from scratch, which reduces response times.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Case Summaries) — summarizes case information for hand-off and review; it does not draft replies to customer chats.
Option C (Case Escalation) — moves cases to higher-level support teams; it is not a generative AI feature and does not address chat response productivity.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=service.einstein_replies_intro.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers wants to implement a customer verification process where sensitive account information can only be accessed after the customer passes identity verification. The agent must enforce this security rule deterministically without allowing the large language model (LLM) to bypass the verification requirement. What should an Agentforce Specialist recommend as the best solution?
optionA: Use context variables to store verification status in the messaging session and configure the agent to check these variables through natural language prompts during each sensitive action.
optionB: Include detailed verification instructions in the agent's topic instructions explaining when customers should be verified and rely on the LLM to follow these guidelines consistently across all interactions.
optionC: Create a custom variable IsCustomerVerified set by a verification action, then apply a conditional filter using the expression IsCustomerVerified equals true to all sensitive data actions, ensuring deterministic access control that the LLM can't alter.
explanation:
Creating a custom variable IsCustomerVerified set by a verification action, then applying a conditional filter with the expression IsCustomerVerified equals true to all sensitive data actions, is the deterministic gate Salesforce gives you for exactly this, and it does not run through the model. You create filters for subagents and actions so that the agent can use them in a conversation only when certain conditions are met, and the condition can be any variable you specify, here a verification variable set by the verification action. For agents on customer channels Salesforce explicitly recommends using filters to require authentication for subagents and actions that perform tasks for a user. A filter is evaluated before the action is available at all, so there is nothing to talk past.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (store verification status in context variables and check them through natural language prompts) — the check becomes part of the reasoning an attacker is trying to talk past; a prompt-level check is probabilistic, not enforced.
Option B (detailed verification instructions in the topic, relying on the LLM) — instructions tell the LLM what should happen and are followed probabilistically, not enforced; the rule stays in the model's hands.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.agent_asset_filters.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers wants its AI agent to answer customer questions with precise and up-to-date information. How does an Agentforce Data Library simplify and enable this?
optionA: It automates the ingestion, taxonomical classification and storage of knowledge in Data Cloud for precision keyword search retrieval to ground prompts and agents with relevant information.
optionB: It automates the ingestion, Indexing of data, and creates a default retriever to be used in prompts and agents for grounding with relevant information.
optionC: It automates the ingestion and optical character recognition (OCR) processing of any PDF, and indexes them to enable regular SQL query retrieval to ground prompts and agents with relevant information.
explanation:
Automating the ingestion and indexing of data and creating a default retriever for prompts and agents is what a data library does. Salesforce describes creating one as automating several configuration steps across Data 360 and Prompt Builder: pushing data streams to Data 360, mapping data objects, and creating a search index and retriever, so linking an agent to your content stops being a manual pipeline build. That retriever is the part that matters at answer time: prompts and agents use it to pull the relevant passages and ground the response in them.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (taxonomical classification for precision keyword search) — data libraries are not a keyword search index with taxonomical classification; retrieval is semantic search over an index built from unstructured and semi-structured content.
Option C (OCR of any PDF for regular SQL query retrieval) — not an OCR-plus-SQL pipeline; the retriever performs semantic search over indexed chunks, not SQL queries.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.data_library_concept.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Choose 1 option. Universal Containers wants to systematically validate agent responses before deployment using a scalable testing process. Which Testing Center approach should the company implement?
optionA: Upload a structured CSV test template and run batch test cases in Testing Center.
optionB: Manually interact with the agent in Builder until responses seem correct.
optionC: Use pilot users in production to flag incorrect responses post-launch.
explanation:
Uploading a structured CSV test template and running batch test cases in Testing Center is the scalable approach. Testing Center is built for scale, and the CSV is how you feed it: Salesforce provides a test template so you can prepare your scenarios as structured data and run them as a batch, and Testing Center then evaluates response accuracy, subagent and action selection, conversation quality, and knowledge retrieval across the whole set. Because agents are non-deterministic, testing across many scenarios is what turns a demo into evidence.
One operational rule goes with this: run the batches in a sandbox, since testing agents can modify CRM data, and expect the runs to consume Einstein Requests either way.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (manually interact in Builder until responses seem correct) — samples a handful of utterances and records nothing you can rerun; not repeatable validation.
Option C (pilot users in production flag incorrect responses post-launch) — moves the discovery of defects to production, where the cost is customer-visible.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.agent_testing_center.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.agent_testing_center_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers wants to be able to detect with a high level confidence if content generated by a large language model (LLM) contains toxic language. Which action should an Al Specialist take in the Trust Layer to confirm toxicity is being appropriately managed?
optionA: Access the Toxicity Detection log in Setup and export all entries where isToxicityDetected is true.
optionB: Create a flow that sends an email to a specified address each time the toxicity score from the response exceeds a predefined threshold.
optionC: Create a Trust Layer audit report within Data Cloud that uses a toxicity detector type filter to display toxic responses and their respective scores.
explanation:
Creating a Trust Layer audit report within Data Cloud that uses a toxicity detector type filter to display toxic responses and their scores is the action, because toxicity is measured by the Trust Layer and reported through audit data, not through a Setup log. Salesforce's guidance is direct: toxicity scores measure the level of potentially harmful language detected by the Einstein Trust Layer in LLM responses, and to monitor toxicity trends in your org you use Einstein Generative AI Audit and Feedback Data, which is stored in Data 360. Reporting on that data with a toxicity filter is what shows the toxic responses alongside their scores.
One detail worth carrying into the exam: isToxicityDetected being true indicates high confidence that the content is toxic, but false does not prove the content is clean; it means only that the model detected nothing.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (export a Toxicity Detection log from Setup) — there is no Toxicity Detection log in Setup to export; the data lives in the audit data model in Data 360.
Option B (a flow that emails when the toxicity score exceeds a threshold) — notifies someone after the fact without establishing that detection is working across responses.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.generative_ai_audit_toxicity.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.generative_ai_feedback.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers wants to use an external large language model (LLM) in Prompt Builder. What should an Agentforce recommend?
optionA: Use Apex to connect to an external LLM and ground the prompt.
optionB: Use BYO-LLM functionality in Einstein Studio.
optionC: Use Flow and External Services to bring data from an external LLM.
explanation:
Using BYO-LLM functionality in Einstein Studio is the supported path. Bring Your Own Large Language Model lets you add a foundation model hosted on an external platform and connect it to Salesforce as a model configuration, which then powers your generative AI, including prompts built in Prompt Builder. You can evaluate the model's responses to your prompts in Model Playground under different settings before deploying it to production.
A naming note: the tool the exam calls Einstein Studio is documented today as AI Models, and its model-building surface is AI Model Builder.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Apex to connect to an external LLM and ground the prompt) — an Apex callout bypasses the model configuration and the Trust Layer handling that comes with a registered model, and Prompt Builder cannot select it as a model.
Option C (Flow and External Services to bring data from an external LLM) — moves data around rather than registering a model that Prompt Builder can select.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=data.c360_a_ai_foundation_models.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: When configuring a prompt template, an Agentforce Specialist previews the results of the prompt template they've written. They see two distinct text outputs: Resolution and Response. Which information does the Resolution text provide?
optionA: It shows the full text that is sent to the Trust Layer.
optionB: It shows the response from the LLM based on the sample record.
optionC: It shows which sensitive data is masked before it is sent to the LLM.
explanation:
Resolution shows the full text that is sent to the Trust Layer. The two outputs in the preview are the prompt and the answer, in that order. Resolution is the resolved prompt: through a process Salesforce calls prompt resolution, Prompt Builder replaces each merge field in the template with real CRM data from the record you selected, so what you are looking at is the full assembled text that leaves Prompt Builder, through the Trust Layer where masking and other policies apply, on its way to the model.
So Resolution answers the question 'what exactly did we send', which is why it is the output you check when a template produces surprising results: a merge field that resolved to the wrong record, or to nothing at all, is visible there and nowhere else.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (the response from the LLM based on the sample record) — that is the Response output, the model's answer to the resolved prompt, not Resolution.
Option C (which sensitive data is masked before it is sent to the LLM) — masking is Trust Layer behaviour, reported through audit data rather than in the template preview; Resolution does not show it.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.prompt_builder_enable_resolution.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.generative_ai_trust_arch.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: B->A. Resolution and Response are two different outputs, and the original key described Response. Salesforce documents resolution as the process that replaces every merge field with real CRM data to produce the resolved prompt — the text that is sent onward — while the response is what the LLM returns.

question: Universal Containers (UC) has recently received an increased number of support cases. As a result, UC has hired more customer support reps and has started to assign some of the ongoing cases to newer reps. Which generative AI solution should the new support reps use to understand the details of a case without reading through each case comment?
optionA: Agent
optionB: Einstein Sales Summaries
optionC: Einstein Work Summaries
explanation:
Einstein Work Summaries is the generative AI solution that lets new customer support reps understand the details of a case without reading through each case comment. Work Summaries use generative AI to provide a concise overview of ongoing cases, summarizing all relevant information in an easily digestible format.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Agent) — an agent can assist with a variety of tasks but is not the feature designed for summarizing an existing case's details for a rep.
Option B (Einstein Sales Summaries) — focused on summarizing sales-related activities such as opportunities and accounts, not support cases.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=service.cc_generative_ai_work_summaries.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers has a custom Agent action calling a flow to retrieve the real-time status of an order from the order fulfillment system. For the given flow, what should the Agentforce Specialist consider about the running user's data access?
optionA: The flow must have the "with sharing" permission selected m the advanced settings for the permissions, field-level security, and sharing settings to be respected.
optionB: The custom action adheres to the permissions, held-level security, and sharing settings configured in the flow.
optionC: The Agent will always run flows in system mode so the running user's data access will not affect the data returned.
explanation:
That the custom action adheres to the permissions, field-level security, and sharing settings configured in the flow is the consideration: the flow's own run context decides what the action can see. Salesforce documents that flows run in user context or system context: in user context the running user's profile and permission sets determine object permissions and field-level access, and in system context access depends on whether the flow runs with sharing or without sharing. A custom agent action calling that flow inherits this; it does not impose a context of its own.
Worth pairing with this: the agent user still needs the Run Flows permission, or access granted to that individual flow, before the action can execute at all.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a "with sharing" permission selected in the flow's advanced settings) — there is no such checkbox to select; the equivalent choice is the flow's run context, of which system context with sharing is one value.
Option C (the Agent always runs flows in system mode) — the agent does not always run flows in system mode, so the running user's access cannot be assumed irrelevant.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.flow_distribute_context.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.agent_actions_common_perms.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: What is the primary function of the reasoning engine in Agentforce?
optionA: Identifying agent topics and actions to respond to user utterances
optionB: Offering real-time natural language response during conversations
optionC: Generating record queries based on conversation history
explanation:
Identifying agent topics and actions to respond to user utterances is the reasoning engine's primary function. The reasoning engine interprets the meaning behind natural language inputs, maps each utterance to the best-matching topic, then evaluates the available actions and selects the one that answers it. For example, if a user asks "What is my current account balance?", the reasoning engine identifies the topic (account information), chooses the correct action (retrieve account balance), executes it and returns the response. It also grounds the response in relevant Salesforce data so the output is accurate and context-aware.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (offering real-time natural language response during conversations) — natural language processing and generation are handled by the large language model, not the reasoning engine, whose job is topic and action selection rather than linguistic processing.
Option C (generating record queries based on conversation history) — query generation is done by an action such as Query Records; the reasoning engine decides which action should run but does not generate queries itself.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.agent_reasoning_engine.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A sales manager needs to contact leads at scale with hyper-relevant solutions and customized communications in the most efficient manner possible. Which Salesforce solution best suits this need?
optionA: Einstein Sales Assistant
optionB: Prompt Builder
optionC: Einstein Lead follow-up
explanation:
Prompt Builder is where personalised outreach gets built once and applied at scale. It ships a Sales Email template type, and Salesforce describes the resulting experience plainly: Einstein pulls in a contact's name and information to customise the email, and unlike a static template it creates a new, personalised output every time. Grounding that template in CRM data is what makes each message hyper-relevant rather than merely mail-merged.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Einstein Sales Assistant) — no sales assistant product replaces the template layer where the content itself is defined; it does not generate the customised communications at scale.
Option C (Einstein Lead follow-up) — lead follow-up features tell a rep which lead to work next rather than generating the communication.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.einstein_sales_emails_draft.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.prompt_builder_standard_template_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An Agentforce is considering using a Field Generation prompt template type. What should the Agentforce Specialist check before creating the Field Generation prompt to ensure it is possible for the field to be enabled for generative AI?
optionA: That the field chosen must be a rich text field with 255 characters or more.
optionB: That the org is set to API version 59 or higher
optionC: That the Lightning page layout where the field will reside has been upgraded to Dynamic Forms
explanation:
That the Lightning page layout where the field will reside has been upgraded to Dynamic Forms is the thing to check. A field generation template writes into a field on a Lightning record page, and that page has to be on Dynamic Forms before an individual field can be enabled for generative AI. Salesforce's procedure says so in its step order: on an existing record page that is not already using Dynamic Forms, you select the Record Detail component and click Upgrade Now, which converts the single block of fields into individual field components; only then can you select a field on the canvas and attach the prompt template to it. On mobile the same requirement appears as enabling Dynamic Forms on Mobile.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a rich text field with 255 characters or more) — an invented prerequisite; there is no 255-character rich-text requirement for the target field.
Option B (org set to API version 59 or higher) — no API version org setting gates the feature.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.prompt_builder_add_field_gen_to_lightning_record_page.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Choose 1 option. Universal Containers (UC) wants to empower its marketing team with Al capabilities that help employees quickly find campaign data, generate creative content, and manage project tasks. The solution should also allow marketers to receive personalized support, surface relevant information, and complete work directly in Salesforce. Which Al solution should UC implement?
optionA: Sales Coach Agent
optionB: Service Agent
optionC: Employee Agent
explanation:
The Employee Agent is the solution. Salesforce's agent type table describes the Employee Agent as assisting employees by providing access to company knowledge, performing tasks, and streamlining workflows across departments, which is this requirement stated back: marketers finding campaign data, generating content, and completing work without leaving Salesforce.
Worth knowing alongside the answer: Employee agents run in employee channels (the Agentforce panel in Lightning Experience, the mobile app, and Slack) and require Flex Credits.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Sales Coach Agent) — works with sales reps on their pitch and role-play, not with a marketing team's tasks.
Option B (Service Agent) — faces customers, supporting them with common inquiries and escalating complex issues; it does not serve internal employees.
References:

question: Universal Containers (UC) wants to use Flow to bring data from unified Data Cloud objects to prompt templates. Which type of flow should UC use?
optionA: Data Cloud-triggered flow
optionB: Template-triggered prompt flow
optionC: Unified-object linking flow
explanation:
A template-triggered prompt flow exists for exactly this job: Salesforce describes it as the way to provide data to prompt templates in Prompt Builder. The flow performs dynamic logic and actions and its output text is merged into the associated prompt template's resolution, which is how data that no simple merge field can reach, including unified Data 360 objects, gets into the prompt.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Data Cloud-triggered flow) — runs when data changes in Data 360; it reacts to data rather than supplying it to a template at resolution time.
Option C (Unified-object linking flow) — there is no such flow type.

question: A Salesforce Administrator wants to generate personalized, targeted emails that incorporate customer interaction data. The admin wants to leverage large language models (LLMs) to write the emails, and wants to reuse templates for different products and customers. Which solution approach should the admin leverage?
optionA: Use sales Email standard templates
optionB: Create a t field Generation prompt template type
optionC: Create a Sales Email prompt template type.
explanation:
Creating a Sales Email prompt template type is the approach. That template type is designed specifically for generating dynamic email content by combining an LLM with a structured template: the admin defines placeholders such as customer name and product details as merge fields, grounds them in customer interaction data, and reuses the same template across products and customers.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (sales Email standard templates) — standard email templates lack LLM integration and dynamic personalization; they merge fields but do not write.
Option B (a "t field Generation" prompt template type) — not a valid prompt template type as printed, and even the real Field Generation type writes a value into a record field rather than composing an email.

question: Which business requirement presents a good use case for leveraging Einstein Prompt Builder?
optionA: Forecast future sales trends based on historical data.
optionB: Identify potential high-value leads for targeted marketing campaigns.
optionC: Send reply to a request for proposal via a personalized email.
explanation:
Sending a reply to a request for proposal via a personalized email is the good use case, because Prompt Builder is a generative tool: it assembles a grounded prompt and has an LLM write text. Drafting a personalised reply to a request for proposal is that shape of problem; the output is language, and the personalisation comes from merge fields resolving against the record.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (forecast future sales trends from historical data) — a predictive problem, a job for a predictive model built and managed as a model rather than as a prompt template; asking an LLM for a forecast would generate prose that looks like a number.
Option B (identify high-value leads for targeted campaigns) — lead scoring is likewise predictive, not generative.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.prompt_builder_standard_template_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.einstein_sales_emails_draft.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Choose 1 option. Universal Containers is setting up the data library configuration within the Agentforce Builder. What is true regarding Agentforce Data Libraries?
optionA: Only data library owners can assign it to the agent.
optionB: Each data category can only have one data library.
optionC: An agent can have only one data library assigned to it.
explanation:
That an agent can have only one data library assigned to it is the true statement. In Agentforce Builder an agent's data source is a single selection: on the agent's Data tab you use the dropdown to select an existing library, and the agent grounds the Answer Questions with Knowledge action on that one library.
What a library is limited to is its data source: a library supports Knowledge, file uploads, or web search, and once you choose a source you cannot change it later.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (only data library owners can assign it) — assignment is a configuration step, not an ownership right; it needs the documented setup permissions rather than being reserved to whoever created the library.
Option B (each data category can only have one data library) — not a documented limit; data categories are not what constrains a library.

question: Universal Containers wants to use an existing prompt template inside Flow as part of automation.
optionA: Invocable Apex
optionB: Einstein for Flow
optionC: Flow action
explanation:
A Flow action is how Flow reaches a prompt template. Salesforce ships a core action for it, Prompt Template Actions, which creates responses based on the LLM response for the specified prompt template and inputs, so in Flow Builder you drop an Action element onto the canvas and select the template you want to run. Note the direction of travel: this is a flow calling a prompt template, the opposite of a template-triggered prompt flow, where the template calls the flow to gather data.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Invocable Apex) — could technically wrap a call, but it is code where a supported clicks-only element already exists.
Option B (Einstein for Flow) — not the mechanism for invoking an existing template; it is a name, not a flow element that runs a prompt template.
