Option C (every modification is saved as a new version automatically) — modifications are not silently versioned for you; a draft keeps taking edits until you activate it.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.prompt_builder_use_multiple_versions.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.prompt_builder_changing_llm_configurations.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is rolling out an AI-powered support assistant to help customer service agents quickly retrieve relevant troubleshooting steps and policy guidelines. The assistant relies on a search index in Data Cloud that contains product manuals, policy documents, and past case resolutions. During testing, UC notices that agents are receiving too many irrelevant results from older product versions that no longer apply. How should UC address this issue?
optionA: Modify the search index to only store documents from the last year and remove older records.
optionB: Create a custom retriever in Einstein Studio, and apply filters for publication date and product line.
optionC: Use the default retriever, as it already searches the entire search index and provides broad coverage.
explanation:
Creating a custom retriever in Einstein Studio and applying filters for publication date and product line is the documented fix. You create an individual retriever, select its search index, define filters, and specify what it returns, so retrieval is confined to the current product line and to documents recent enough to apply. Where relevance also depends on age, hybrid search lets you configure ranking factors such as recency, using a field like LastModifiedDate on the indexed object.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (modify the index to store only the last year and remove older records) — would work only by destroying history that other cases still need, and it treats the index as a store rather than as a view over the source content, which it is not.
Option C (use the default retriever for broad coverage) — the default retriever is the cause here, not the cure; it searches the whole index, which is exactly why superseded manuals keep surfacing.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=data.c360_a_ai_retriever_create.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.data_library_custom_retriever.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=data.c360_a_hybridsearch_fusion_ranking.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: C->B. The original key recommended keeping the default retriever, whose whole-index coverage is what produces the irrelevant results described. Salesforce documents the custom retriever as the way to narrow retrieval — select the search index, define filters, specify what is returned — with recency ranking available as a hybrid search ranking factor.

question: Universal Containers (UC) is building a Flex prompt template. UC needs to use data returned by the flow in the prompt template. Which flow element should UC use?
optionA: Add Flex Instructions
optionB: Add Prompt Instructions
optionC: Add Flow Instructions
explanation:
Add Prompt Instructions is the element. Salesforce defines it as providing data in the form of prompt instructions that are merged into a prompt template in Prompt Builder, and it exists only in template-triggered prompt flows, which is exactly the arrangement here: a flow supplying data to a flex template. The text and resources it evaluates at run time are stored in the $Output global variable, and that output is what lands in the template.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Add Flex Instructions) — no such element exists; the name is an invention built from the surrounding vocabulary.
Option C (Add Flow Instructions) — likewise not a flow element.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.flow_ref_elements_add_prompt.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.flow_concepts_trigger_prompt_template_capability.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: C->B. Salesforce documents one element for this job and names it Add Prompt Instructions. Neither Add Flow Instructions nor Add Flex Instructions exists in Flow Builder, so the original key named a non-existent element.

question: In Model Playground, which hyperparameters of an existing Salesforce-enabled foundational model can an Agentforce change?
optionA: Temperature, Frequency Penalty, Presence Penalty
optionB: Temperature, Top-k sampling, Presence Penalty
optionC: Temperature, Frequency Penalty, Output Tokens
explanation:
Temperature, Frequency Penalty and Presence Penalty are the hyperparameters. Model Playground is where you evaluate a model's response to your prompts under different settings before deploying it, and the settings it exposes for a Salesforce-enabled foundation model are temperature, frequency penalty, and presence penalty. Salesforce's own worked example uses exactly these three when it tells you how to reproduce the standard sales email behaviour in a model configuration: temperature 1.0, frequencyPenalty 1.0, presencePenalty 0.5, on gpt-3.5-turbo.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Temperature, Top-k sampling, Presence Penalty) — top-k sampling is not among the exposed hyperparameters.
Option C (Temperature, Frequency Penalty, Output Tokens) — output token limits are a property of the model and the request rather than a Model Playground control.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=data.c360_a_ai_foundation_models.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.prompt_builder_standard_prompt_templates.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers built a Field Generation prompt template that worked for many records, but users are reporting random failures with token limit errors. What is the cause of the random nature of this error?
optionA: The template type needs to be switched to Flex to accommodate the variable amount of tokens generated by the prompt grounding.
optionB: The number of tokens generated by the dynamic nature of the prompt template will vary by record.
optionC: The number of tokens that can be processed by the LLM varies with total user demand.
explanation:
The number of tokens generated by the dynamic nature of the prompt template varying by record is the cause, because the prompt is not a fixed string; it is assembled per record. Grounding replaces each merge field with that record's real data, so an account with a long description, many related list rows, or a verbose flow output produces a far larger resolved prompt than a sparse one. The token budget covers the resolved prompt plus the generated response, so the same template sails through on most records and trips the limit on the fat ones. That is what makes the failures look random when they are not.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (switch the template type to Flex) — changes how inputs are defined, not how many tokens a record's data occupies.
Option C (the LLM's token capacity varies with total user demand) — the model's context window is a fixed property of the model, not something that shrinks as other customers get busy.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.prompt_builder_ground_template.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.prompt_builder_enable_resolution.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Which use case is best supported by Salesforce Agent's capabilities?
optionA: Bring together a conversational interface for interacting with AI for all Salesforce users, such as developers and ecommerce retailers.
optionB: Enable Salesforce admin users to create and train custom large language models (LLMs) using CRM data.
optionC: Enable data scientists to train predictive AI models with historical CRM data using built-in machine learning capabilities
explanation:
Bringing together a conversational interface for interacting with AI for all Salesforce users is the use case Agentforce supports. It is a conversational layer over the platform: a user states what they want, the reasoning engine classifies the request into a topic and runs the actions that fulfil it, calling Apex, flows, and prompt templates along the way. It is offered across the Salesforce estate rather than to one audience, with agent types for service, sales, employees, and admins.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (admins create and train custom LLMs using CRM data) — building and training custom LLMs is not an admin activity; external models are connected through Bring Your Own LLM rather than trained in Salesforce.
Option C (data scientists train predictive models on historical CRM data) — that is the job of AI Model Builder in Data 360, not of an agent.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.agent_reasoning_engine.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.agent_setup_explore_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A support team handles a high volume of chat interactions and needs a solution to provide quick, relevant responses to customer inquiries. Responses must be grounded in the organization's knowledge base to maintain consistency and accuracy. Which feature in Einstein for Service should the support team use?
optionA: Einstein Service Replies
optionB: Einstein Reply Recommendations
optionC: Einstein Knowledge Recommendations
explanation:
Einstein Service Replies is the feature. It is the generative feature for live conversations: it drafts fluent replies for reps during chat and messaging sessions from the conversation's context, and Salesforce's instruction is to add grounding to Service Replies with Service AI Grounding or an Agentforce Data Library so the recommendations come from your Knowledge base. That combination is what keeps high-volume chat both fast and consistent with published policy.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Einstein Reply Recommendations) — the predictive predecessor; it surfaces replies learned from your org's closed chat transcripts, with no generative model and no Knowledge grounding.
Option C (Einstein Knowledge Recommendations) — surfaces articles for the rep to read rather than drafting the response.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=service.einstein_replies_intro.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=service.einstein_generative_ai_enable_grounding.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) needs to save agents time with AI-generated case summaries. UC has implemented the Work Summary feature. What does Einstein consider when generating a summary?
optionA: Generation is grounded with conversation context, Knowledge articles, and cases.
optionB: Generation is grounded with existing conversation context only.
optionC: Generation is grounded with conversation context and Knowledge articles.
explanation:
Generation grounded with conversation context, Knowledge articles, and cases is the keyed answer: a work summary starts from the conversation and is enriched by case data. Einstein predicts and fills a summary, issue, and resolution at the end of a rep-customer conversation or from the Case page, and Service AI Grounding adds the case as a grounding source: case fields, comments, and the case feed (system updates, user comments, email messages, and status changes) are used to give Einstein details for drafting a case summary.
One precision worth carrying: in Salesforce's grounding table, Knowledge appears as a grounding source for Service Replies for Email rather than for case summaries. Treat the Knowledge half of this answer as the exam's framing rather than as a documented grounding source for Work Summaries.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (conversation context only) — the summary is not built from the transcript alone; case fields, comments and the case feed are documented grounding sources.
Option C (conversation context and Knowledge articles) — omits the case, which is the grounding source Salesforce actually documents for case summaries.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=service.cc_generative_ai_work_summaries.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=service.einstein_generative_ai_grounding_setup.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) wants to ensure the effectiveness, reliability, and trust of its agents prior to deploying them in production. UC would like to efficiently test a large and repeatable number of utterances. What should the Agentforce Specialist recommend?
optionA: Leverage the Agent Large Language Model (LLM) UI and test UC's agents with different utterances prior to activating the agent.
optionB: Deploy the agent in a QA sandbox environment and review the Utterance Analysis reports to review effectiveness.
optionC: Create a CSV file with UC's test cases in Agentforce Testing Center using the testing template.
explanation:
Creating a CSV file with UC's test cases in Agentforce Testing Center using the testing template is the recommendation, because Testing Center is built for volume: it supports large-scale batch testing and Salesforce provides a CSV template so you can upload your own scenarios and run them as a batch, evaluating response accuracy, subagent and action selection, and knowledge retrieval. That is what makes a large, repeatable set of utterances practical before go-live.
One operational rule to remember with it: run tests in a sandbox, since testing agents can modify CRM data, and expect the runs to consume Einstein Requests in either environment.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (test utterances in the Agent LLM UI before activating) — typing utterances one at a time into a preview cannot cover a repeatable suite.
Option B (deploy to a QA sandbox and review Utterance Analysis reports) — measures what happened after the fact rather than validating expected behaviour ahead of activation.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.agent_testing_center.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.agent_testing_center_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: What is the primary advantage of creating an individual retriever instead of the default retriever?
optionA: Individual retrievers can aggregate multiple data spaces and data model objects (DMOs) into a unified retriever output.
optionB: Individual retrievers allow the configuration of filters, specified fields, and how many results are returned.
optionC: Individual retrievers automatically generate new search indexes and dynamically update vectors.
explanation:
Allowing the configuration of filters, specified fields, and how many results are returned is the advantage. Salesforce describes an individual retriever by exactly what you get to control: you create it to improve the relevancy of content returned to a prompt, and you customise it by selecting its search index, defining filters, and specifying what information it returns. The default retriever gives you none of those levers; it searches its index broadly and returns what it finds.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (aggregate multiple data spaces and DMOs into a unified output) — an individual retriever fetches from one search index; aggregating across several is what an ensemble retriever is for.
Option C (automatically generate search indexes and update vectors) — retrievers do not create search indexes or maintain vectors; indexing is a separate process that a retriever reads from.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=data.c360_a_ai_retriever_create.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=data.c360_a_ai_retriever_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An Agentforce is setting up a new org and needs to ensure that users can create and execute prompt templates. The Agentforce Specialist is unsure which roles are necessary for these tasks. Which permission sets should the Agentforce Specialist assign to users who need to create and execute prompt templates?
optionA: Prompt Template Manager for creating templates and Data Cloud Admin for executing templates
optionB: Prompt Template Manager for creating templates and Prompt Template User for executing templates
optionC: Data Cloud Admin for creating templates and Prompt Template User for executing templates
explanation:
Prompt Template Manager for creating templates and Prompt Template User for executing templates are the two permission sets. Prompt Template Manager is the permission Salesforce lists for creating or modifying prompt templates, and Prompt Template User is what a person needs to access and run prompt templates outside Prompt Builder, which is what 'execute' means here.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Prompt Template Manager and Data Cloud Admin for executing) — Data Cloud permissions govern models, retrievers, and Data 360 objects; a Data Cloud admin permission set is not what lets an end user run a template.
Option C (Data Cloud Admin for creating and Prompt Template User for executing) — a Data Cloud admin permission set does not confer the ability to author a template.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.copilot_actions_custom.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.prompt_builder_add_field_gen_to_lightning_record_page.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers plans to enhance the customer support team's productivity using AI. Which specific use case necessitates the use of Prompt Builder?
optionA: Creating a draft of a support bulletin post for new product patches
optionB: Creating an Al-generated customer support agent performance score
optionC: Estimating support ticket volume based on historical data and seasonal trends
explanation:
Creating a draft of a support bulletin post for new product patches is the use case that necessitates Prompt Builder, because Prompt Builder is for generating language grounded in your data, and this is the one whose output is text: the bulletin, assembled from the patch's record data and written in a consistent voice each time.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (an AI-generated agent performance score) — a predictive problem, model territory built and managed in AI Model Builder in Data 360; an LLM asked for a score yields prose shaped like a number rather than a prediction.
Option C (estimating ticket volume from history and seasonality) — likewise a forecast, which is a predictive model's job, not a prompt template's.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.prompt_builder_standard_template_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=data.c360_a_ai_license_perms.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Which part of the Einstein Trust Layer architecture leverages an organization's own data within a large language model (LLM) prompt to confidently return relevant and accurate responses?
optionA: Prompt Defense
optionB: Data Masking
optionC: Dynamic Grounding
explanation:
Dynamic Grounding is the part of the architecture that puts your data into the prompt. Salesforce describes secure data retrieval and grounding as the first thing the Trust Layer does: the LLM needs context from your CRM data to generate a relevant, personalised response, and grounding is the process of adding that context, through merge fields drawn from record fields, flows, Apex, Data 360 DMOs, and related lists. It is 'secure' because retrieval respects the executing user's permissions, role-based controls, and field-level security.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Prompt Defense) — applies system policies that steer the model away from unintended or harmful output; it protects the exchange rather than enriching it with data.
Option B (Data Masking) — replaces sensitive values with placeholders before the prompt leaves Salesforce; it removes data from the prompt rather than adding it.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.generative_ai_trust_arch.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An Agentforce Specialist created a Field Generation prompt template. What should the Agentforce Specialist do to expose the template to the user?
optionA: Use a screen flow to associate the Field Generation prompt template.
optionB: Associate the template with the form field on the Lightning page.
optionC: Call a template using an autolaunched flow.
explanation:
Associating the template with the form field on the Lightning page is how a field generation template is exposed: by attaching it to the field itself. In Lightning App Builder you open the record page, make sure it uses Dynamic Forms (clicking Upgrade Now on the Record Detail component if it does not), then select the field on the canvas and associate the prompt template with it. The user then gets a button on that field that populates it with generated content.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a screen flow to associate the template) — a screen flow would build a separate interface rather than enabling the field; no flow is involved.
Option C (call the template using an autolaunched flow) — an autolaunched flow can call a prompt template as automation but does not put the generation control in front of the user on the record.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.prompt_builder_add_field_gen_to_lightning_record_page.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: What is an appropriate use case for leveraging Agentforce Sales Agent in a sales context?
optionA: Enable a sates team to use natural language to invoke defined sales tasks grounded in relevant data and be able to ensure company policies are applied. conversationally and in the now or work.
optionB: Enable a sales team by providing them with an interactive step-by-step guide based on business rules to ensure accurate data entry into Salesforce and help close deals fatter.
optionC: Instantly review and read incoming messages or emails that are then logged to the correct opportunity, contact, and account records to provide a full view of customer interactions and communications.
explanation:
Enabling a sales team to use natural language to invoke defined sales tasks grounded in relevant data, with company policies applied conversationally in the flow of work, is the appropriate use case. The value of an agent in sales is that a rep can ask for something in their own words and have the platform do the defined work: the reasoning engine classifies the request into a topic and runs the actions assigned to it, grounded in CRM data, with filters and instructions keeping it inside company rules.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (an interactive step-by-step guide for accurate data entry) — a guided path for data entry is guidance and validation, not an agent.
Option C (instantly review and log incoming messages to the right records) — that is activity capture, which runs quietly in the background rather than responding to what a rep asks for.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.agent_reasoning_engine.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.sales_cloud_agents.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Coral Cloud Resorts (CCR) wants to configure its agent so that booking actions are only available when a customer's membership tier is "Premium" or "Elite". This business rule must be enforced deterministically. What should CCR implement?
optionA: Set up custom validation rules on the underlying booking objects to prevent non-eligible customers from completing bookings.
optionB: Configure topic instructions that clearly state booking actions should only be used for Premium or Elite customers and include examples.
optionC: Create a context variable mapped to the customer's membership tier field, then add a conditional filter on MembershipTier.
explanation:
Creating a context variable mapped to the customer's membership tier field and adding a conditional filter on MembershipTier is what CCR should implement, because deterministic means the rule is enforced before the model gets a say, and filters are how Agentforce does that. You add the variable holding the membership tier to the agent's context, then create a filter so the booking actions are available in a conversation only when that variable meets the condition. Salesforce recommends exactly this pattern for customer channels, where filters are used to require authentication for actions that perform tasks for a user.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (validation rules on the booking objects) — prevents bad records, but only at save time; the agent would still offer and attempt the booking, and the customer would meet an error instead of a boundary.
Option B (topic instructions stating the rule with examples) — guidance the LLM usually follows, which is not the same as an action being unavailable; it cannot give a deterministic guarantee.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.agent_asset_filters.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is implementing Agentforce Service Agent on Email, UC made an email template and now needs to connect it to a Service Agent. What should an Agentforce Specialist recommend?
optionA: Create an Email Configuration for the Service Agent.
optionB: Create an Omni-Channel flow to point to an email template.
optionC: No action needed; the Service Agent connects automatically.
explanation:
Creating an Email Configuration for the Service Agent is the recommendation, because Salesforce names the connecting object directly: the email configuration connects your email template to an Agentforce Service agent. You create it in Setup and then link it to one or more routing addresses, which is what puts the agent on the inbound email channel.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (an Omni-Channel flow pointing to an email template) — an Omni-Channel flow is the routing mechanism for messaging work, not the way an email template is bound to a Service agent.
Option C (no action needed) — nothing happens automatically; an agent does not attach itself to email.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.service_agent_email_configuration.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.service_agent_considerations_1.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is creating a new custom prompt template to populate a field with generated output. UC enabled the Einstein Trust Layer to ensure AI Audit data is captured and monitored for adoption and possible enhancements. Which prompt template type should UC use and which consideration should UC review?
optionA: Field Generation, and that Dynamic Fields is enabled
optionB: Field Generation, and that Dynamic Forms is enabled
optionC: Flex, and that Dynamic Fields is enabled
explanation:
Field Generation, with Dynamic Forms enabled, is the template type and the consideration. Populating a field with generated output is what a field generation template does, so the question turns on the prerequisite, and the documented prerequisite is Dynamic Forms. Salesforce's procedure makes it a required step: on a record page that is not already using Dynamic Forms you select the Record Detail component and click Upgrade Now, which converts the block of fields into individual field components, and only then can a field be associated with the prompt template. On mobile the same requirement appears as enabling dynamic forms on mobile.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Field Generation, and that Dynamic Fields is enabled) — there is no Salesforce feature called Dynamic Fields, which is what rules out the original key.
Option C (Flex, and that Dynamic Fields is enabled) — a flex template would not populate the field: flex is for use cases the standard types do not cover, and it does not attach to a field on a record page; and Dynamic Fields does not exist.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.prompt_builder_add_field_gen_to_lightning_record_page.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.salesforce_app_field_gen.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: A->B. Both options name the correct template type, and the discriminator is the consideration. Salesforce documents Dynamic Forms as the prerequisite for enabling a field for generative AI — Upgrade Now on the Record Detail component, and dynamic forms on mobile for the mobile app. Dynamic Fields is not a Salesforce feature.

question: An Agentforce Specialist builds a new Service Agent that uses a custom action built on a flow. The agent has been tested in a sandbox and is now ready to deploy. What is a key consideration regarding the activation status of the agent in the production environment?
optionA: The agent will be activated automatically only if the flow is also active.
optionB: The agent must be manually activated in production, regardless of its status in the sandbox.
optionC: The agent will automatically be activated upon successful deployment.
explanation:
That the agent must be manually activated in production, regardless of its status in the sandbox, is the key consideration: deployment moves metadata, it does not turn the agent on. Activating an agent is its own step; Salesforce describes activation as what makes the agent available to your customers or employees once it is deployed to one or more channels, so a sandbox agent that was active arrives in production inactive and stays that way until someone activates it there.
Two rules that come with activation are worth knowing: only one version of an agent can be active at a time, and activating a new version replaces the currently active one. That is what makes the zero-downtime pattern work.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (activated automatically only if the flow is also active) — an active flow is required for the custom action to run, but it does not activate the agent.
Option C (activated automatically upon successful deployment) — deployment never activates an agent; activation is a separate manual step in the target org.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.copilot_setup_activate_deactivate.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.prompt_builder_considerations_changeset.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Which configuration must an Agentforce complete for users to access generative Al-enabled fields in the Salesforce mobile app?
optionA: Enable Mobile Generative AI.
optionB: Enable Mobile Prompt Responses.
optionC: Enable Dynamic Forms on Mobile.
explanation:
Enabling Dynamic Forms on Mobile is the configuration. Salesforce's procedure for the mobile app opens with this step: enable dynamic forms on mobile, then add the prompt template to the Lightning record page. The same requirement appears as a note alongside the desktop instructions: for users to access generative AI-enabled fields in the Salesforce mobile app, you must first enable Dynamic Forms on Mobile.
The reason is structural rather than AI-specific. A generative AI-enabled field is an individual field component on the page, and only Dynamic Forms renders fields individually; without it the mobile app shows the old single block of record details with no per-field control to invoke.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Enable Mobile Generative AI) — not a setting in Salesforce.
Option B (Enable Mobile Prompt Responses) — not a setting in Salesforce either.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.salesforce_app_field_gen.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.prompt_builder_add_field_gen_to_lightning_record_page.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: A->C. Salesforce's mobile procedure begins 'Enable dynamic forms on mobile', and the desktop article repeats it as the prerequisite for accessing generative AI-enabled fields in the mobile app. The original key named a Mobile Generative AI setting that does not exist.

question: Sales reps at Universal Containers should not be able to create or edit prompt templates. Which permission set should an Agentforce Specialist assign to the sales reps?
optionA: Prompt Execute User
optionB: Prompt Template Manager
optionC: Prompt Template User
explanation:
Prompt Template User is the permission set. Prompt Builder has two permission sets, and the one that runs templates without authoring them is Prompt Template User: Salesforce lists it for accessing and running prompt templates outside Prompt Builder, carrying Execute Prompt Templates. So reps who should use templates but never change them get Prompt Template User.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Prompt Execute User) — there is no Prompt Execute User permission set in Salesforce, which is what makes the original key impossible to assign.
Option B (Prompt Template Manager) — adds Manage Prompt Templates, the create-and-edit rights these reps are supposed not to have.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.prompt_builder_enable.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.prompt_builder_add_field_gen_to_lightning_record_page.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: A->C. Salesforce documents exactly two Prompt Builder permission sets: Prompt Template Manager (create and manage) and Prompt Template User (run templates outside Prompt Builder). Prompt Execute User does not exist, so the original key named an unassignable permission set.

question: Choose 1 option. Universal Containers has PDF maintenance guides in an external folder, not yet in Salesforce. The team wants a standard, clicks- only setup for the Service Agent to use these documents. Which approach should the Agentforce Specialist implement?
optionA: Paste external PDF links into topic instructions and rely on the model to follow them, avoiding configuration of a retrieval source, index, or retriever action.
optionB: Upload the PDFs as File source in the Agentforce Data Library which will build a Search Index, and create a retriever to ground responses from those documents.
optionC: Configure Data Cloud to ingest file attachments and create custom index and retriever for product record and attachment data.
explanation:
Uploading the PDFs as a File source in the Agentforce Data Library, which builds a search index, and creating a retriever to ground responses from those documents is what a data library is for. You choose files as the library's data source and upload the PDFs, and creating the library automates the rest (pushing data streams to Data 360, mapping the objects, and building a search index and retriever), so the Service Agent can ground answers on those documents through the Answer Questions with Knowledge action. It is configuration, not code, which is what a clicks-only requirement asks for.
One thing to plan for: a library's data source is fixed once chosen (Knowledge, file uploads, or web search), so a file-based library stays file-based.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (paste external PDF links into topic instructions) — gives the model URLs it cannot fetch, so responses stay ungrounded.
Option C (Data Cloud attachment ingestion with a custom index and retriever) — would work, but it is the manual version of what the data library does for you, and these PDFs are not attached to Salesforce records at all.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.data_library_concept.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.data_library_select_fields.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: At Universal Containers, a sales manager is tackling a tough challenge as several new junior sales reps struggle with objection handling and price negotiations for complex deals. The manager lacks the time to personally guide each sales rep through their specific customer scenarios before their critical meetings. The junior sales reps have asked for a tool that would allow them to practice their pitches by simulating tough conversations and receive personalized feedback that is specific to the commerce opportunity they are working on. Which Salesforce solution should an Agentforce Specialist recommend?
optionA: Employee Coach
optionB: SDR Agent
optionC: Sales Coach
explanation:
Sales Coach is the documented agent for this: Salesforce describes it as intelligently giving reps personalised, actionable, stage-specific feedback on their sales pitch or role-play session. Practising objection handling against a simulated buyer and getting feedback tied to the opportunity in front of them is the use case it exists for.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Employee Coach) — there is no Employee Coach agent in the agent type table.
Option B (SDR Agent) — the Lead Nurturing agent, the exam's SDR agent, engages prospects by email and books meetings; it never coaches a rep.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.agent_setup_explore_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.sales_cloud_agents.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is expanding its Agentforce for Service capabilities to include case management. For security purposes, UC wants the agent to verify a customer's identity before providing any case-related information. The verification must be deterministic-ensuring that no case details are shared unless identity verification has been successfully completed. Which approach best meets this requirement?
optionA: Use keywords such as "Always" and "Never" to write clear logic in Topic Instructions to verify user identity before providing any case information,
optionB: Create a variable to store the verification status, set it as output from a "Verify Identity" action, and apply a filter so any case-related actions only run when the variable confirms verification.
optionC: Store the verification status in a custom variable and set a global instruction that the agent should check this variable before sharing case information.
explanation:
Creating a variable to store the verification status, setting it as output from a Verify Identity action, and applying a filter so case-related actions only run when the variable confirms verification is the approach, because determinism comes from a filter, not from wording. Salesforce's documented mechanism is exactly this: filters that make subagents and actions usable in a conversation only when conditions on a variable are met, and it recommends them for requiring authentication on customer channels. A filter removes the action from consideration entirely, so there is no instruction for a determined customer to argue past.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Always and Never keywords in Topic Instructions) — an instruction is guidance to the model however it is phrased; the model usually complies, and 'usually' is what this requirement rules out.
Option C (a custom variable plus a global instruction to check it) — stores the right state but enforces it through an instruction, which has the same flaw: the check runs inside the model's reasoning rather than gating the action.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.agent_asset_filters.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A data science team has trained an XGBoost classification model for product recommendations on Databricks. The Agentforce Specialist is tasked with bringing inferences for product recommendations from this model into Data Cloud as a stand-alone data model object (DMO). How should the Agentforce Specialist set this up?
optionA: Create the serving endpoint in Databricks, then configure the model using Model Builder.
optionB: Create the serving endpoint in Einstein Studio, then configure the model using Model Builder.
optionC: Create the serving endpoint in Databricks, then configure the model using a Python SDK connector.
explanation:
Creating the serving endpoint in Databricks, then configuring the model using Model Builder, is the setup: build and serve in Databricks, connect and consume in Salesforce. You set up the serving endpoint in Databricks (that is the connection point Salesforce documents between Databricks and Data 360) and then connect that model on the Salesforce side to define prediction criteria and land the inferences as a DMO you can use.
Naming note: the tool the exam calls Model Builder is now AI Model Builder, formerly Einstein Studio Model Builder, and it sits under Data 360.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (create the serving endpoint in Einstein Studio) — the endpoint belongs to the platform hosting the model; Salesforce's role is to consume it with a zero-copy approach rather than to host the model.
Option C (configure the model using a Python SDK connector) — no Python SDK connector is part of the documented path.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=data.c360_a_ai_byom_set_up_your_endpoint_databricks.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=data.c360_a_ai_byom_connect_your_external_model_databricks.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=data.c360_a_bring_your_own_model.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An Agentforce Specialist wants to ensure their custom agent action performs as expected in conversations. What should the Agentforce Specialist focus on when creating action instructions?
optionA: Write concise agent action instructions and test in Agentforce Builder.
optionB: Ensure the agent action label matches the utterance's intent.
optionC: Include comprehensive detailed descriptions and perform smoke testing.
explanation:
Writing concise agent action instructions and testing in Agentforce Builder is the focus. Action instructions tell the agent what the action does and when to use it, and Salesforce's guidance is to plan them carefully and then test, which is what Agentforce Builder's Preview panel is for, since it shows which subagents and actions an utterance selected and the reasoning behind the selection. Write tightly, then watch what the reasoning engine actually picks.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (make the action label match the utterance's intent) — the label is not matched against an utterance; the model weighs names and instructions together against the conversation.
Option C (comprehensive detailed descriptions and smoke testing) — piling on detail is not the goal; long, redundant instructions blur the boundary between one action and the next, which is the failure mode that makes an agent call the wrong thing.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.copilot_actions_instructions.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.agent_builder_tour.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) wants its AI agent to return responses quickly. UC needs to optimize the retriever's configuration to ensure minimal latency when grounding AI responses. Which configuration aspect should UC prioritize?
optionA: Configure the retriever to operate in dynamic mode so that it modifies the search Index structure at runtime.
optionB: Ensure the retriever's filters are defined to limit the scope of each search efficiently.
optionC: Increase the recency bias setting for the retriever limiting scope to more recent data.
explanation:
Ensuring the retriever's filters are defined to limit the scope of each search efficiently is the aspect to prioritise, because latency in retrieval is mostly a function of how much has to be searched and returned. An individual retriever is configured by selecting its search index, defining filters, and specifying what information it returns; narrow the eligible set and both the search and the prompt assembly get shorter.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (dynamic mode that modifies the search index at runtime) — there is no such mode; indexing is a separate process the retriever reads from.
Option C (increase the recency bias to limit scope) — recency is a ranking factor in hybrid search: it reorders results rather than reducing how many are considered, so it changes what comes first, not how fast.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=data.c360_a_ai_retriever_create.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=data.c360_a_hybridsearch_fusion_ranking.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: What is one key purpose of action instructions when creating a custom agent action in Agentforce?
optionA: Action instructions help the reasoning engine decide which action to use.
optionB: Action instructions define the temperature of the large language model (LLM) powering the Reasoning Engine.
optionC: Action instructions tell the user how to call this action in a conversation.
explanation:
Helping the reasoning engine decide which action to use is the purpose of action instructions; they are read by the machine, not by the user. Salesforce defines action instructions as telling the agent what your action does and when to use it, and the reasoning engine collects the names and instructions of a subagent's actions, including input and output instructions, when it decides what to do next. Good instructions are therefore the difference between an action that gets chosen at the right moment and one that never fires.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (define the LLM's temperature) — temperature is a hyperparameter of the model configuration, not something instructions set.
Option C (tell the user how to call the action) — instructions are not user-facing documentation; a user never sees them and does not call actions by name.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.copilot_actions_instructions.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.agent_reasoning_engine.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: After creating a foundation model in Einstein Studio, which hyperparameter should an Agentforce use to adjust the balance between consistency and randomness of a response?
optionA: Presence Penally
optionB: Variability
optionC: Temperature
explanation:
Temperature is the consistency dial. In a model configuration it governs how deterministic the output is: lower values keep responses close to the most probable continuation, higher values allow more variation. Salesforce's own reproduction recipe for the standard sales email behaviour sets it explicitly, alongside frequency and presence penalties, in a model configuration you build and evaluate in Model Playground.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Presence Penalty) — discourages reusing tokens that have already appeared, which shapes repetition rather than randomness.
Option B (Variability) — not a hyperparameter Salesforce exposes.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=data.c360_a_ai_foundation_models.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.prompt_builder_standard_prompt_templates.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Choose 1 option. Universal Containers has created an Employee Agent. Which step should an Agentforce Specialist take to connect the agent with a Slack channel?
optionA: Create a connection between Salesforce and the Slack workspace.
optionB: Create an Omni-Channel flow and connection between Salesforce and the Slack workspace.
optionC: Create an embedded service deployment and connection between Salesforce and the Slack workspace.
explanation:
Creating a connection between Salesforce and the Slack workspace is the step. Employee agents run in employee channels, and Slack is one of them: Salesforce's instruction is to add the Slack connection to your agent and then finish setting up the agent in Slack, which rests on the Salesforce org being connected to the Slack workspace, with users holding the permission that links the two.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (an Omni-Channel flow plus the connection) — an Omni-Channel flow routes work to queues and agents in service scenarios; it is customer-channel machinery, not how an Employee agent reaches Slack.
Option C (an embedded service deployment plus the connection) — an embedded service deployment puts a chat window on a website; it has nothing to do with Slack.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.agent_deploy_emp_slack.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.agent_setup_explore_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An Agentforce is tasked with analyzing Agent interactions looking into user inputs, requests, and queries to identify patterns and trends. What functionality allows the AX Specialist to achieve this?
optionA: User Utterances dashboard
optionB: Agent Event Logs dashboard
optionC: AI Audit & Feedback Data dashboard
explanation:
The User Utterances dashboard is the functionality, and the feature behind it is Utterance Analysis, which answers exactly this question: it lets you see how users are using agents, what they are requesting, and whether the agent was able to handle those requests, through customisable reports that help you refine subagents and actions. It lives as a dashboard in the Agentforce (Default) folder on the Dashboards tab, tracking users along with the input and the agent's response type, and it refreshes weekly from reports run at the weekend.
One caveat with a date on it: Agentforce Analytics, which Utterance Analysis belongs to, is scheduled for retirement starting May 2026, with Agent Analytics as the replacement.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Agent Event Logs dashboard) — there is no agent event logs dashboard; end-to-end execution detail comes from Agentforce Session Tracing.
Option C (AI Audit & Feedback Data dashboard) — audit and feedback data records Trust Layer behaviour such as masking and toxicity rather than request patterns.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.copilot_utterance_analysis.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.generative_ai_session_trace_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Which element in the Omni-Channel Flow should be used to connect the flow with the agent?
optionA: Route Work Action
optionB: Assignment
optionC: Decision
explanation:
The Route Work action is the element that hands the conversation to its destination in an Omni-Channel flow: it is where you choose the agent, queue, or skill that should take the work. That is how a messaging conversation reaches an Agentforce Service agent.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Assignment) — a general flow element that sets variable values; it routes nothing.
Option C (Decision) — a general flow element that branches the path; it may appear in the same flow, but it does not connect the flow to an agent.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.service_agent_escalation.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.agent_parent_deploy.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: The marketing team at Universal Containers is looking for a way personalize emails based on customer behavior, preferences, and purchase history. Why should the team use Agent as the solution?
optionA: To generate relevant content when engaging with each customer
optionB: To analyze past campaign performance
optionC: To send automated emails to all customers
explanation:
Generating relevant content when engaging with each customer is why the team should use Agent. The requirement is personalised content per customer, and that is generation grounded in data: the prompt merges the customer's behaviour, preferences, and purchase history into the template, and the model writes an email shaped by that record rather than by a static block of copy. Salesforce's description of generated sales email is the same idea: unlike a static template, it creates a new, personalised output every time.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (analyze past campaign performance) — reporting, not generative work.
Option C (send automated emails to all customers) — blasting the same email to everyone is precisely the undifferentiated approach personalisation is meant to replace.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.einstein_sales_emails_draft.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.prompt_builder_ground_template.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers is building an Agentforce Service Agent to handle order cancellations. The Agentforce Specialist needs to ensure that a critical "Check Cancellation Eligibility" action is executed deterministically on every relevant turn, without relying on the reasoning engine's discretion to choose the tool. During a code review, a junior developer asks why the Agentforce Specialist called the action using the run @actions.name command instead of simply listing the action under the reasoning.actions block. What must the Agentforce Specialist explain regarding the difference between these two invocation methods?
optionA: Both patterns execute the action on every turn automatically; the difference is purely syntactic, as the run command is simply the newer notation for Agent Script.
optionB: The run command is only valid when nested inside reasoning.actions blocks to pass parameters; the Agentforce Specialist must list it under reasoning.actions for the large language model (LLM) to access it.
optionC: Listing an action under reasoning.actions makes it a subjective tool that the large language model (LLM) decides whether to call; calling it with the run command forces guaranteed execution every time.
explanation:
Listing an action under reasoning.actions makes it a subjective tool the LLM decides whether to call, while calling it with the run command forces guaranteed execution every time. Salesforce's Agent Script actions reference draws exactly this line: an action called explicitly from the logic section of a subagent's reasoning "is run every time the subagent is run", while an action exposed in reasoning.actions is passed to the LLM, which "can subjectively choose to run the tool based on the current context". A mandatory eligibility check belongs in the logic, not in the LLM's tool list.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (both patterns run every turn; the difference is syntax) — only the run form is deterministic; a tool in reasoning.actions runs only if the LLM picks it.
Option B (run is only valid nested inside reasoning.actions) — backwards; run belongs in the reasoning logic, and inside reasoning.actions it is used only to chain an action after a tool the LLM chose.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/ai/agentforce/guide/ascript-ref-actions.html

question: When configuring a file upload-based Data Library, what are the maximum allowed file sizes for text or HTML files and PDF files, respectively?
optionA: Up to 100 MB for text or HTML files and up to 4 MB for PDF files
optionB: Up to 50 MB for both text or HTML files and PDF files
optionC: Up to 4 MB for text or HTML files and up to 100 MB for PDF files
explanation:
Up to 4 MB for text or HTML files and up to 100 MB for PDF files is the documented limit. Salesforce's Use Uploaded Files page says "Text and HTML files can be up to 4MB, and PDF files can be up to 100 MB", with up to 1,000 files per library.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (100 MB for text or HTML, 4 MB for PDF) — the two limits reversed.
Option B (50 MB for both) — no uniform limit exists; the limit differs by file type.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.data_library_file_upload.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An Agentforce Specialist wants to use the related lists from an account in a custom prompt template. What should the Agentforce Specialist consider when configuring the prompt template?
optionA: The text encoding (for example, UTF-8, ASCII) option
optionB: The maximum number of related list merge fields
optionC: The choice between XML and JSON rendering formats for the list
explanation:
The maximum number of related list merge fields is the consideration. Prompt Builder Limits caps a template at 5 related-list merge fields (alongside 50 merge fields in total, 5 flow merge fields and 5 Apex merge fields), so a template that pulls several Account related lists can run into it. The related list's fields come from the parent object's page layout for the current user.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (the text encoding option) — Prompt Builder has no encoding setting for related lists.
Option C (a choice between XML and JSON rendering) — there is no choice; Salesforce documents that related-list data "is rendered in JSON format".
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.prompt_builder_limits.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.prompt_builder_ground_related_list.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is implementing Einstein Generative AI to improve customer insights and interactions. UC needs audit and feedback data to be accessible for reporting purposes. What is a consideration for this requirement?
optionA: Storing this data requires Data Cloud to be provisioned.
optionB: Storing this data requires a custom object for data to be configured.
optionC: Storing this data requires Salesforce big objects.
explanation:
Storing this data requires Data Cloud (now Data 360) to be provisioned. Salesforce's Audit Trail page says "Audit trail along with feedback data is stored in Data 360", and that to access it you turn on Einstein generative AI data collection and storage and install the report package, then report on it with Data 360 reports.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (a custom object) — the audit and feedback data lands in Data 360 automatically; no custom object is involved.
Option C (big objects) — not where generative AI audit data is stored.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.generative_ai_audit_trail.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Once a data source is chosen for an Agentforce Data Library, what is true about changing that data source later?
optionA: The data source can be changed through the Data Cloud settings.
optionB: The Data Retriever can be reconfigured to use a different data source.
optionC: The data source cannot be changed after it is selected.
explanation:
The data source cannot be changed after it is selected. Salesforce says it plainly on the data library setup pages: "After you select a library's data source, you can't change it later." To switch source you create a new library.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (change it through Data Cloud settings) — no such setting; the lock is on the library itself.
Option B (reconfigure the Data Retriever) — the retriever is generated from the library's source and does not re-point the library.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.data_library_file_upload.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.data_library_select_fields.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An Agentforce Specialist is working declaratively on version 4 of a prompt template, which is significantly different than the previous version 3. A bug is then identified in version 3 and requires a hotfix to be deployed to production immediately by another team. The team will deploy this change as a new version. What should the specialist do to ensure that their work on the latest version is not lost and does not conflict with the new version?
optionA: Create a new prompt template with the bug fix, update all references to the new version, and delete the old prompt template.
optionB: Save their work in version 4, and allow the template to be deployed with a new version 5 containing the fix.
optionC: Copy and paste version 4 into a backup file or version-control alternative, and allow the other team to overwrite the contents of version 4 with the bug-fixed version.
explanation:
Save the work in version 4 and let the fix be deployed as a new version 5. Prompt Builder keeps each version separately: Save As, then Save as a New Version creates the next version without touching the current one, and "Activating a template version makes it immutable", so the hotfix can go live as version 5 while version 4's draft survives.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (new template, repoint references, delete the old one) — unnecessary churn; versioning exists to avoid exactly this.
Option C (back up version 4 and let the other team overwrite it) — overwriting a version throws away work that versioning would have kept for free.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.prompt_builder_use_multiple_versions.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers plans to enhance its sales team's productivity using AI. Which specific requirement necessitates the use of Prompt Builder?
optionA: Creating a draft newsletter for an upcoming tradeshow.
optionB: Predicting the likelihood of customers churning or discontinuing their relationship with the company.
optionC: Creating an estimated Customer Lifetime Value (CLV) with historical purchase data.
explanation:
Creating a draft newsletter for an upcoming tradeshow is the requirement that needs Prompt Builder, because it is the only one whose output is generated text. Prompt Builder's template types all produce language — emails, field content, summaries, flex content — grounded in your data.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (predicting churn likelihood) — a predictive score, which is model territory (AI Models / Model Builder), not prompt generation.
Option C (estimating Customer Lifetime Value) — also a numeric prediction from historical data, not a language task.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.prompt_builder_standard_template_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers is building an Agentforce Service Agent to help customers track their purchases. To store the customer's order number during the conversation, the Agentforce Specialist creates and initializes a variable in Agent Script using the declaration order_id: string = "", omitting the mutable keyword. During testing, the agent attempts to update this variable with the user's order number via the @utils.setVariables utility. What is the result of this variable declaration at runtime?
optionA: The variable defaults to mutable; the mutable keyword is optional and has no effect, allowing the agent to successfully update the variable.
optionB: The declaration is a syntax error and the agent will fail to deploy.
optionC: The variable is treated as read-only; it cannot be updated by actions or @utils.setVariables at runtime because it lacks the mutable keyword.
explanation:
The variable is treated as read-only and cannot be updated at runtime, because it lacks the mutable keyword. The Agent Script variables reference defines mutable as the keyword that "Allows the agent to change the variable's value. To ensure a variable's value is never changed, define the variable without mutable." To capture the order number it must be declared order_id: mutable string = "".
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (mutable is the default and optional) — the reverse of the documented behaviour.
Option B (a syntax error that blocks deployment) — declaring a variable without mutable is valid; it simply makes the variable read-only.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/ai/agentforce/guide/ascript-ref-variables.html

question: Universal Containers is developing an Agentforce Service Agent to handle a complex, multi-step customer onboarding process. To better organize the conversational logic, the Agentforce Specialist splits the process across two distinct subagents and places the setup configuration for the second step inside the before_reasoning block of the new subagent. During testing, when the agent transitions to this new subagent mid-conversation, the conversation occasionally stalls or behaves unexpectedly. What is the risk the Agentforce Specialist must consider regarding the execution timing of before_reasoning?
optionA: The before_reasoning block will only run once and sets the immutable variables.
optionB: The before_reasoning block runs at the start of the next turn after a transition.
optionC: The before_reasoning block only runs on the very first turn after the agent launches.
explanation:
The before_reasoning block running at the start of the next turn after a transition is the exam's answer, and it is the only option that is not plainly false — but read this item with care, because Salesforce's documentation does not state it. The Agent Script reference says a transition "executes immediately when encountered", that Agentforce then "reads the second subagent from top to bottom", and that before_reasoning "is functionally equivalent to adding logic to the beginning of a subagent's instructions" and runs on every request. Read together, that suggests the target subagent's setup logic is processed in the same request as the transition. The practical lesson either way: do not assume setup placed in a target subagent has already run at the moment of a mid-conversation transition, and verify the timing in Agentforce Builder's preview.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (runs only once and sets immutable variables) — before_reasoning runs on every request to the subagent, and it can set mutable variables.
Option C (runs only on the very first turn after launch) — also contradicted; it is part of every pass through the subagent.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/ai/agentforce/guide/ascript-ref-before-after-reasoning.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/ai/agentforce/guide/ascript-flow.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/ai/agentforce/guide/ascript-ref-utils.html

corrected.note: Kept as the exam key, but no Salesforce page states that before_reasoning waits for the next turn after a transition. The Agent Script reference points the other way: a transition "executes immediately", Agentforce "reads the second subagent from top to bottom", and before_reasoning is "functionally equivalent to adding logic to the beginning of a subagent's instructions". Treat the item as testing the exam writer's model rather than a documented rule.

question: An AI Specialist is tasked with configuring a generative model to create personalized sales emails using customer data stored in Salesforce. The AI Specialist has already fine-tuned a large language model (LLM) on the OpenAI platform. Security and data privacy are critical concerns for the client. How should the Agentforce Specialist integrate the custom LLM into Salesforce?
optionA: Create an application of the custom LLM and embed it in Sales Cloud via iFrame.
optionB: Add the fine-tuned LLM in Einstein Studio Model Builder.
optionC: Enable model endpoint on OpenAI and make callouts to the model to generate emails.
explanation:
Adding the fine-tuned LLM in Einstein Studio Model Builder (now AI Models) is the secure integration. Salesforce's developer guide says you can "bring your own large language model (BYOLLM) from an LLM provider using your own account", after which the model is saved to the Model Library as a foundation model you can configure — so prompts to it pass through the Einstein Trust Layer like any other model.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (embed a custom app via iFrame) — bypasses the Trust Layer and Salesforce's data controls entirely.
Option C (call the OpenAI endpoint directly) — a hand-built callout loses masking, audit and grounding; BYOLLM exists so you do not have to do this.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/einstein/genai/guide/get-started-einstein-studio.html

question: Cloud Kicks uses a third-party agent for research and an Agentforce agent for customer service. Which purpose-built protocol allows cross-vendor agents to communicate?
optionA: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
optionB: Application Programming Interface (API)
optionC: Agent-to-Agent (A2A)
explanation:
Agent-to-Agent (A2A) is the purpose-built protocol for cross-vendor agents. Salesforce defines it as "an open standard that allows AI agents across different platforms to discover one another, communicate securely, and coordinate work", and positions it for task delegation between agents.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Model Context Protocol) — MCP connects an agent to tools, data and APIs, not to another agent.
Option B (a generic API) — an API integrates systems but is not a protocol for agents to discover and collaborate with each other.
References:
https://www.salesforce.com/agentforce/ai-agents/agent2agent-protocol/
https://www.salesforce.com/blog/how-to-choose-integration-pattern-for-agentforce/
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/ai/agentforce/guide/mcp.html

question: An Agentforce Specialist turned on Einstein Generative AI in Setup. Now, the Agentforce Specialist would like to create custom prompt templates in Prompt Builder. However, they cannot access Prompt Builder in the Setup menu. What is causing the problem?
optionA: The Prompt Template User permission set was not assigned correctly.
optionB: The Prompt Template Manager permission set was not assigned correctly.
optionC: The large language model (LLM) was not configured correctly in Data Cloud.
explanation:
The Prompt Template Manager permission set not being assigned is the cause. Prompt Builder's own pages list "Prompt Template Manager permission set" as the permission needed "To create and manage prompt templates in Prompt Builder"; without it the Prompt Builder node does not appear in Setup even with Einstein generative AI turned on.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Prompt Template User) — that set lets users run templates, not build them.
Option C (the LLM configured in Data Cloud) — standard models need no Data Cloud configuration, and a model problem would not hide the Setup menu.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.prompt_builder_use_multiple_versions.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: At Horizon Insurance, the customer service team is reporting that the agent consistently routes claims intake conversations to the Policy Inquiry subagent, even though user intent clearly indicates a claims-related issue. This misrouting persists despite the user clearly expressing the intent to discuss a claim. The Agentforce Specialist added guard conditions, but the problem persists. What is most likely causing this incorrect routing in Horizon Insurance's agent?
optionA: Procedural instructions requiring Salesforce Flows to route to the correct subagent
optionB: Use of global instructions to define subagent routing for agents in compliance-regulated environments
optionC: Overlap in subagent descriptions and entry conditions between the Claims Intake and Policy Inquiry subagents
explanation:
Overlap in subagent descriptions and entry conditions between Claims Intake and Policy Inquiry is the likely cause. Salesforce's context-engineering guide says the reasoning engine "matches a customer message to the most appropriate subagent based on its name and description" and that "Clear and distinct subagents prevent overlap and ensure the Reasoning Engine correctly classifies customer requests." Guard conditions do not help when both subagents' descriptions claim the same intent.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (procedural instructions requiring Flows to route) — routing is done by the reasoning engine from subagent descriptions, not by flows.
Option B (global instructions in regulated environments) — there is no such routing rule; this names a context, not a cause.
References:
https://www.salesforce.com/agentforce/guide/

question: The Agentforce Specialist for Cloud Kicks wants to create an agent that will allow the sales staff to schedule their daily tasks and assist in providing detailed explanations behind product prices and deals. Following Salesforce best practices, which type of agent should they create?
optionA: Service Agent
optionB: Employee Agent
optionC: Sales Agent
explanation:
An Employee Agent is the type to create, because the users are Cloud Kicks' own sales staff scheduling their own tasks and asking for internal explanations of prices and deals. Salesforce's Agent Types and Considerations describes the Employee Agent as one that "Assists employees by providing access to company knowledge, performing tasks, and streamlining workflows across departments". "Sales Agent" is not an agent type on that list — the sales-focused types are Engagement (formerly Lead Nurturing/SDR), which works leads, and Sales Coach, which gives reps pitch feedback.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Service Agent) — built to support external customers with common inquiries and escalations, not internal staff.
Option C (Sales Agent) — not a documented agent type; the requirement is internal productivity, which is the Employee Agent's job.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.agent_setup_explore_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: The dump keyed Sales Agent, which is not an agent type. Salesforce's Agent Types and Considerations lists Employee Agent, Engagement (formerly Lead Nurturing/SDR), Sales Coach, Service Agent, Service Assistant and Setup with Agentforce; an agent that helps internal sales staff with their own tasks is an Employee Agent, which "Assists employees by providing access to company knowledge, performing tasks, and streamlining workflows".

question: Universal Containers needs to ground a new Agentforce agent with structured data stored in an external system without duplicating it in Data 360. This approach is necessary to ensure real-time data accuracy and minimize storage costs. Which Data 360 concept should the team use to accomplish this?
optionA: Establish a semantic index for external content.
optionB: Utilize Zero Copy to access external data without ingestion.
optionC: Configure a data stream to import the data into Data 360.
explanation:
Using Zero Copy to access external data without ingestion is the right concept. Salesforce's Zero Copy Data Federation page says federation queries physically distinct sources as one logical system and "avoids duplicating data across system boundaries"; the resulting data lake object is a pointer to the external table rather than a copy, which keeps the data current and avoids storage cost.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a semantic index for external content) — an index supports meaning-based retrieval but does not solve access-without-copying.
Option C (a data stream that imports the data) — ingestion is the duplication the requirement rules out.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=data.c360_a_byol_data_federation.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is discussing its AI strategy in an agile Scrum meeting. Which business requirement would lead an Agentforce Specialist to recommend connecting to an external foundational model via Einstein Studio (Model Builder)?
optionA: UC wants to fine-tune model temperature.
optionB: UC wants a model fine-tuned using company data.
optionC: UC wants to change the frequency penalty of the model.
explanation:
UC wanting a model fine-tuned using company data is the requirement that needs an external foundation model. Bring Your Own LLM lets you connect a model from a provider "using your own account" and use it as a foundation model in AI Models (formerly Einstein Studio), so a model fine-tuned on UC's data can serve Salesforce prompts.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (tune the temperature) — a model configuration setting available on standard models; no external model needed.
Option C (change the frequency penalty) — likewise a generation parameter, set in a model configuration or at invocation.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/einstein/genai/guide/get-started-einstein-studio.html

question: An Agentforce Specialist created a custom Agent action, but it is not being picked up by the planner service in the correct order. Which adjustment should the AI Specialist make in the custom Agent action instructions for the planner service to work as expected?
optionA: Specify the dependent actions with the reference to the action API name.
optionB: Specify the profiles or custom permissions allowed to invoke the action.
optionC: Specify the LLM model provider and version to be used to invoke the action.
explanation:
Specifying the dependent actions by their action API name is the adjustment. Best Practices for Agent Action Instructions lists "Dependent actions" as something to add when needed: "If a required action is missing from a plan or actions aren't being called in the right order, you can specify them by API name", for example "If the IdentifyRecordByName action is part of the plan, it must run before GetRecordFieldsAndValues."
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (profiles or custom permissions allowed to invoke it) — access control, which does not affect ordering.
Option C (the LLM provider and version) — action instructions do not choose the model.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.copilot_actions_instructions.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: How should an organization use the Einstein Trust layer to audit, track, and view masked data?
optionA: Utilize the audit trail that captures and stores all LLM submitted prompts in Data Cloud.
optionB: In Setup, use Prompt Builder to send a prompt to the LLM requesting for the masked data.
optionC: Access the audit trail in Setup and export all user-generated prompts.
explanation:
Utilizing the audit trail that captures and stores all LLM-submitted prompts in Data Cloud is how you audit masked data. Salesforce's Audit Trail page says generative AI audit data "includes data about the Einstein Trust Layer features such as data masking and toxicity scores", is "stored in Data 360", and that when masking is on it "includes the masked prompt text that was sent to an external LLM".
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (ask the LLM for the masked data in Prompt Builder) — the model never received the unmasked values, and this is not an audit mechanism.
Option C (the audit trail in Setup, exported) — the Setup Audit Trail logs configuration changes, not prompts; Prompt Builder activity is not even tracked there.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.generative_ai_audit_trail.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A sales rep at Universal Containers is extremely busy and sometimes will have very long sales calls on voice and video calls and might miss key details. They are just starting to adopt new generative AI features. Which Einstein Generative AI feature should an Agentforce Specialist recommend to help the rep get the details they might have missed during a conversation?
optionA: Call Summary
optionB: Call Explorer
optionC: Sales Summary
explanation:
Call Summary is the feature. Einstein Conversation Insights users "can access generative call summaries and generative insights on voice and video calls", and a standard call summary includes the summary itself, the customer impression and next steps — exactly what a rep who missed details needs.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Call Explorer) — a tool for exploring and searching call data (Salesforce recommends testing insights in it), not a summary of one call.
